📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in two days, federal authorities filed suits against two states that treat prediction markets as illegal gambling. The cases could decide whether state gaming regulators or the CFTC control sports event contracts, which compete with licensed sportsbooks and online casinos.

The federal government has opened two upcoming court fights with states over prediction markets. Both target state actions against event contracts offered on CFTC-regulated exchanges. Arkansas and Louisiana treat those contracts as illegal gambling. Washington argues that federal law takes priority.

In a recent development, the Arkansas complaint carries case number 4:26-cv-01255-BSM. It is aimed at the enforcement action Griffin filed against KalshiEX LLC and Kalshi Inc. That state suit alleges multiple violations of the Arkansas Deceptive Trade Practices Act. It seeks restitution, penalties, taxes and injunctive relief.

According to recent reports, in release 9325-26, the CFTC mentioned Arkansas could seek civil penalties against CFTC-registered exchanges that could reach hundreds of millions of dollars. The federal suit also aims to stop the state from halting event-contract trading. The government wants a preliminary and permanent injunction. That order would bar Arkansas officials from investigating CFTC-regulated entities, their affiliates and partners. It would also stop them from enforcing state law against those firms over transactions on designated contract markets.

Griffin’s stance is not new. In October 2025, he issued a formal opinion that sports event contracts are gambling and require a license. The new case brings the preemption fight into the Eighth Circuit, which has not yet ruled on the question.

According to recent reports, with Arkansas added, the CFTC’s tally of state lawsuits over federal authority reaches 11. The agency has also filed amicus briefs in four federal appeals courts and one state supreme court.

The Louisiana case moved within a day. Judge Jeffrey Johnson of the 21st Judicial District Court in Tangipahoa Parish signed the restraining order. The named entities are linked to Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood, Crypto.com, Coinbase, Gemini, ForecastEx, Novig, Underdog, IG Group and ProphetX.

Industry observers note that in release 9326-26, the CFTC remarked the order shut down more than 30 companies tied to CFTC-regulated derivatives without giving them notice or a chance to be heard. The federal suit was filed in the Eastern District of Louisiana. It names the state, Attorney General Liz Murrill, the Louisiana Gaming Control Board and the state police gaming enforcement division. It asks the court to declare state gambling laws preempted. It also seeks to stop Louisiana from enforcing or extending the state order.

🚨Breaking: Louisiana judge orders temporary restraining order prohibiting Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood, and other “prediction market” operators from continuing their unlicensed and unregulated illegal gambling in Louisiana.

It’s not complicated: if you aren’t a… pic.twitter.com/gzrQlN9CCL.

Sources indicate that the exchange between officials has been sharp. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig described Louisiana’s emergency suit as “naked lawfare and a cynical political stunt.” On Nov. 14, Murrill answered on X. She accused Selig of “flatly false statements” and argued that states have regulated gambling for 250 years.

For licensed sportsbooks and online casinos, the outcome matters directly. If federal preemption holds, sports event contracts could operate outside state gaming rules in both states. The federal requests to block both states’ actions now go before the U.S. District Courts for the Eastern Districts of Arkansas and Louisiana.

Latest Update: Security incident disclosure — July 2026

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1120 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure.
  • We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services.
  • Industry observers note that the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

Industry observers note that the intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

In a recent development, the campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

Industry observers note that we are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the glitch and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

According to recent reports, as a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

Sources indicate that we are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

Recent findings suggest that to understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that maine's Gambling Control Unit is heading toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos after a single public hearing. A former lawmaker warns that the state's behavioral health system is too thin for a possible rise in gambling addiction, while a federal lawsuit still targets the tribes' exclusivity.

It has been revealed that maine’s regulator is moving toward an early 2027 launch of tribal-run online casinos. Only one public hearing has been held so far. WGME’s I-Team reported on Nov. 16 that the Gambling Control Unit began iGaming rulemaking in June. Residents in the report raised a separate concern. They worry the state lacks the mental health and problem-gambling resources to cope.

Industry observers note that maine will become the eighth state with legal online casinos. Its four Wabanaki tribes hold exclusive licenses under LD 1164, the Wabanaki internet gaming act. The Legislature lists the measure as enacted as Public Law 538.

The money set aside for addiction services is small next to the state’s cut. The legislative fiscal note sends 2% of adjusted gross iGaming receipts to the Gambling Addiction Prevention and Treatment Fund. The state’s own 18% share is projected at $1.8 million in fiscal 2025-26 and $3.6 million in fiscal 2026-27.

According to recent reports, critics doubt the system can absorb the demand. Patty Locuratolo Hymanson, a neurologist and former state lawmaker, told WGME that Maine lacks the behavioral health resources to handle a possible rise in gambling addiction from online casinos.

Recent findings suggest that lawmakers reshaped the revenue split before passage. A committee amendment raised the state’s share from 16% to 18%. The same amendment cut the opioid treatment fund’s allocation from 3% to 1.5%. The fiscal note also carries ongoing General Fund appropriations of $645,354 for six Gambling Control Unit positions. Those include two criminal intelligence analysts and two auditors.

The regulator itself was skeptical at first. Before the bill became law, Executive Director Milt Champion opposed it in written testimony. He argued iGaming wasn’t warranted while sports wagering was only in its second year.

Rulemaking is still underway. The unit issued its third version of the draft rules on Sept. 30, 2026, and took comments until Oct. 30. Champion has warned that major revisions would force a fourth publication. The third draft keeps the tax rate on adjusted gross receipts unchanged. It also retains the license fee and bond requirements. The regulator is hiring six staff members dedicated to iGaming.

In a recent development, the launch also faces a court fight over tribal exclusivity. Churchill Downs and Oxford Casino Hotel brought their suit against the Gambling Control Unit and Champion in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maine. They are asking the court to declare the law unconstitutional. The challenge goes to the heart of the market’s design, which reserves online casino licenses for the tribes.

It has been revealed that the next deadlines are procedural. Under Maine’s rulemaking law, the unit has up to 120 days after comments close to adopt the rules. The Attorney General’s office has up to 150 days from that same date to approve them as legal. The unit’s rulemaking page also lists a public hearing notice marked Nov. 30, 2026, which could change that timetable.

  • Industry observers note that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Online casinos supplied most of the growth in Pennsylvania's October 2026 gaming revenue, while sports betting handle slipped. The results land as a stalled bill to ban sweepstakes casinos and raise sports betting taxes runs out of time.

Recent findings suggest that pennsylvania’s gaming revenue reached $634.4 million in October 2026, up 6.3% from a year earlier and the highest monthly total on record. Online casinos contributed a record $278.8 million, up 11.1%. The total cleared the previous single-month mark of $625.5 million, which was set in May 2026.

Industry observers note that iGaming accounted for about $27.7 million of the $37.4 million year-over-year increase. A year earlier, online casino revenue was $251,097,586, itself a record at the time. Total gaming tax revenue in October 2025 was $252,287,937, against a record $274 million this October.

According to recent reports, two licensees led the iGaming field. Hollywood Casino at Penn National generated $114.4 million, up 16%. Valley Forge Casino Resort followed with $75.2 million, up 5.3%.

October was a stronger month than September. In September, total gaming revenue was $555,036,870, a 4.07% year-over-year increase. iGaming table revenue slipped 0.63% that month.

In a recent development, the October pattern mirrors the last fiscal year. iGaming revenue in fiscal 2025/26 was $2,933,453,989, an 18.42% gain over the prior year. It generated $1,337,414,660 in tax. Combined gaming revenue reached $7,005,987,435, an all-time fiscal-year high. Taxes and fees returned to the state totaled $3,098,193,583.

Recent findings suggest that pennsylvania’s online casino growth is in line with a slowing iGaming trend nationally. US iGaming revenue rose 12.3% year over year to $1.03 billion in August 2026. For the state budget, the vertical is now a central source of gaming tax.

Sports betting moved the other way on volume. Handle fell to $903 million from $968.5 million in October 2025. Revenue still rose, to $65.1 million from $60.7 million. The same split indicated up across fiscal 2025/26. Handle dropped from $8,721,795,533 to $8,448,101,928. Sports wagering revenue rose 35.95% to $662,947,631.

The record arrives as Harrisburg weighs a gaming modernization package. Rep. Russ Diamond introduced House Bill 2801 with four co-sponsors. On September 24, 2026, it was referred to the House Gaming Oversight Committee. Titled ‘Skill Games & Gaming Modernization,’ the bill would rewrite large parts of the state’s gaming code.

According to recent reports, house Bill 2801 would make operating or promoting online sweepstakes games illegal in Pennsylvania. Fines would range from $50,000 to $500,000 per violation.

It has been revealed that the bill would also raise the sports wagering tax from 34% to 36%. The state currently taxes online slots at 54%. A higher sports rate would apply to a product whose handle is shrinking even as its revenue climbs.

The bill has not moved. HB 2801 had no recorded committee hearing or vote as of mid-November, according to Legal Sports Report. The legislative session ends November 30. Bills that do not pass by then do not carry into 2027.

#207236. Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1411 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Css-tricks ↗ Open Full Page

Taming Typography: Building a Modern CSS Reset

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1411 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Css-tricks

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset.
  • I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.
  • Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CSS can now make choices about type that used to sit outside a reset. text-wrap: pretty can prevent a stranded word, container query units can scale a heading to the column it occupies, and text-box can trim the half-leading built into a line box. Some of these features are experimental and browser support is uneven, so they need guardrails rather than blind inclusion.

I’ve put together tidy-typography.css, which gathers the useful parts into a default stylesheet: rendering and fallback rules, fluid sizing, vertical rhythm, wrapping, hyphenation, and OpenType detail.

Use it whole, or take the declaration that solves the particular irritation in front of you. I’ll walk you through all the details in this article and give you the full code at the end.

font-synthesis: none stops a browser from inventing bold or italic when the family lacks that face. The smoothing and text-rendering declarations are rendering hints, mainly for WebKit; results still vary by platform.

Industry observers note that text-size-adjust disables mobile font inflation that can make a deliberately sized layout jump on rotation. font-size-adjust: from-font uses font metrics to reduce the apparent size change while a fallback swaps for a webfont.

(As with other snippets in this article, this ⁠:root block is a partial excerpt the final stylesheet combines it with additional custom properties defined later on.).

Viewport-based fluid type does not know how wide its element is. A heading in a narrow sidebar can therefore scale as though it fills the viewport.

According to recent reports, container-type: inline-size makes the wrapper a container query, so its children can use cqi: a unit based on the container rather than the viewport. Replacing vw in clamp() lets the same heading scale appropriately in an article column or a 300px sidebar without component-specific media queries.

In a recent development, line-height includes space above the cap-height and below the baseline: half-leading. It becomes obvious when text must align tightly with another element. text-box-trim removes it, while text-box-edge measures from capital-letter caps to the alphabetic baseline. This is a metrics-aware alternative to font-specific negative-margin nudges.

Selectors Level 5 proposes :heading, matching h1 to h6 and [role="heading"]. It has not landed in browsers, so keep it behind an @supports selector() check.

Default heading wrapping can leave one short final line. text-wrap: balance distributes text across its lines and works best for blocks of up to about six lines. For paragraphs, text-wrap: pretty avoids a stranded final word without balancing the whole block. Both replace JavaScript orphan fixers. Editable text needs text-wrap: stable, which prevents each newly introduced word from reshuffling the paragraph.

hyphens: auto relies on the browser’s language dictionaries, so the document needs a correct lang attribute (for example ). Without one the browser has no dictionary to use and won’t be able to hyphenate text. Even with the correct lang, the defaults can leave tiny word fragments or several hyphenated lines in a row.

It has been revealed that hyphenate-limit-chars controls the smallest breakable word and fragments; hyphenate-limit-lines prevents a ladder effect. hyphenate-limit-zone makes breaks less frequent, while hyphenate-limit-last protects the final word. Safari needs the prefixed equivalents, so declare both sets together.

Set code, variables, and headings to hyphens: manual: a broken code word can change meaning, and a hyphenated heading usually reads as an error.

Punctuation marks don’t carry the same visual weight as letters, so a quotation mark sitting at the start of a line can look slightly indented against the text below it. hanging-punctuation lets specified punctuation sit fractionally outside the text block’s edge.

The first value handles opening punctuation, and last handles closing punctuation at the end of a block, while allow-end lets punctuation hang past the right edge rather than force-wrapping. The result is a text block whose edges read as genuinely flush.

Underlines have a related problem. Browsers apply flat, one-size-fits-all thickness and position regardless of the font’s actual weight.

Sources indicate that text-decoration-thickness: from-font reads the thickness the font’s designer intended. text-underline-offset gives descenders room to breathe, and text-decoration-skip-ink: auto interrupts the underline wherever a descender crosses it rather than drawing straight through the letter.

Variable fonts often include an optical size axis, or opsz. It lets a typeface use thinner strokes at large display sizes and thicker, more legible strokes when set small.

In a recent development, font-optical-sizing: auto lets the font make that adjustment based on its actual rendered size. The @supports block covers the older font-variation-settings syntax some browsers still need, while font-variant-ligatures and font-kerning enable the font’s own ligatures and kerning pairs.

Light text on a dark background genuinely reads heavier than the same weight on a light background. Where a font ships a GRAD, or grade, axis, the dark mode block dials that perceived weight down without changing glyph shape or width the way an actual weight change would. Fonts without a GRAD axis safely ignore the setting.

It has been revealed that mixing a monospace font into running prose often exposes a mismatched x-height at the same declared font-size. The size-adjust keyword, set once at the @font-face level, scales that font’s rendered output specifically, leaving the actual font-size value untouched.

Numbers in a table need identical widths so they stack into a clean column on the screen. Conversely, numbers in flowing text don’t need the same treatment and should sit naturally alongside the surrounding words.

It has been revealed that the tabular-nums and lining-nums keywords give table digits a fixed width and full cap height. oldstyle-nums and proportional-nums let digits sit alongside lowercase letters without sticking up and disrupting the sentence’s texture.

Recent findings suggest that font-variant-emoji makes the choice between full-colour and monochrome emoji explicit. Without it, the browser or platform gets to choose a fallback, and the result can vary more than you expect. Apply .emoji-color or .emoji-mono to containers where you want to enforce that choice, rather than setting it globally on the body.

Quote style and character order differ by language and region. English nests single quotes inside double quotes, British English reverses that convention, and French uses guillemets with a thin space.

According to recent reports, the quotes property declares the order for each language through :lang(). The native q element then inserts the right pair through open-quote and close-quote. The same markup can render correctly in each locale without hardcoding characters into the content.

Wrapping the rules in :where() keeps them at zero specificity, so a project can override the quote style with one plain class.

Default sub and sup styling is synthesized. The browser just shrinks the text and shifts the baseline, rather than using glyphs actually designed for that position.

Industry observers note that font-variant-position switches to the font’s own purpose-built sub and superscript glyphs where they exist, resetting vertical-align, font-size, and line-height so they don’t fight against the real glyph’s intended size and position. Most typefaces only include proper numerals rather than letters, so check the specific font before applying this broadly.

:where() always resolves to zero specificity, which is useful for a reset. Every rule here is an opinionated default, and wrapping it in :where() lets a project override a property with a plain class.

Sources indicate that :is() solves a different problem: repetition. The heading selector list appears several times in a typographic stylesheet, and grouping it avoids the risk of forgetting a level.

Unlike :where(), :is() carries the specificity of its most specific argument.

Industry observers note that here’s the complete reset, combining the stable layers. Unsupported declarations are ignored by the browser, so the stylesheet can be adopted gradually.

Much of this CSS removes work that used to leak into other parts of a build. text-wrap can take over orphan handling from JavaScript, container query units keep a component’s type scale tied to its own width, and text-box-trim avoids the negative margins once used to compensate for leading. quotes, font-variant-position, and font-optical-sizing hand several smaller details back to the language and the font instead of a collection of one-off fixes.

Browser support will continue to change, especially for text-wrap and text-box-trim. Unsupported declarations are ignored, but that only helps when the unenhanced typography is acceptable in its own right.

Some of these rules are still too new for a baseline reset. A news article, a marketing page, and an editable product interface do not ask the same things of their text; the set that belongs in yours depends on the font, the content, and the browsers you still need to support.

#207235. Newer Models, Same Advantage

📅 16 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2080 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Newer Models, Same Advantage

📅 16 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models.
  • Industry observers note that the training pipeline was built in two stages.
  • The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

Industry observers note that the training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving swiftly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

Industry observers note that that concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — fresh architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two latest OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

Recent findings suggest that dharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

According to recent reports, processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Industry observers note that figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'.

According to recent reports, these are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

Recent findings suggest that the examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Sources indicate that extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

Sources indicate that when a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output.

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

Sources indicate that the operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Recent findings suggest that mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Recent findings suggest that supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

Industry observers note that the benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

Sources indicate that this is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — upcoming architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Recent findings suggest that better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we revealed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

Because these events produced no system crashes or logging errors, the teams behind these agents had no way to know until the damage occurred.

Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Platform watches for exactly these concerns. It reads the traces and logs your agents already produce and flags sessions where an agent goes outside the job it was built for.

Before you point it at your production agents, you'll probably want to see it work in a test environment. In this hands-on guide, we’ll walk you step-by-step through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection and using it to capture your very first agent behavior anomaly. By the end of this post, you'll have:.

However, it has a deliberate flaw: the agent has access to an overprivileged fetch_records tool which can read any table, including a `payroll` table containing sensitive employee data. All three parts of the lethal trifecta are here: the agent can read private data, it takes input from people it can't vet, and it sends what it finds back in its reply. Tool permissions and guardrails should stop most of this, but they only block what someone thought to write down. Agent Anomaly Detection flags the sessions that get past them, usually within a few minutes.

Michigan's online casinos generated $305.3 million in adjusted gross receipts in October, up 16.7% from a year earlier. The double-digit gain comes as national iGaming growth cools, though Michigan's own pace has slowed from a year ago.

It has been revealed that michigan’s online casino market kept growing at a double-digit rate in October. Gross receipts came to $318.1 million, according to figures the Michigan Gaming Control Board released Nov. 18. It was the state’s second-best iGaming month of 2026. Only March, with a record $309.1 million in AGR, was higher. March also holds the monthly gross receipts record of $322.1 million, which topped the $315.8 million from December 2025.

The October result followed a soft patch. September AGR was $288.15 million, 0.9% lower than in August.

The year-over-year gain stands out against the national backdrop. Citizens JMP Securities estimated that US iGaming revenue grew 12% in the third quarter of 2026, the slowest pace it has recorded. Growth had been 19% in the first quarter and 16% in the second. The same data put Michigan’s third-quarter iGaming growth at 17%. Only Delaware, at 36%, and West Virginia, at 26%, grew faster.

Recent findings suggest that michigan’s own pace has still slowed sharply. In October 2025, online casino AGR grew 31.8% year over year, nearly double this October’s rate. That month produced $261.7 million in AGR and $278.5 million in gross receipts, a record at the time.

Recent findings suggest that the Michigan figures also invite comparison with Pennsylvania. Its online casinos generated $278,845,570 in October revenue, a state record for Pennsylvania. That figure came in a release issued Nov. 17, a day before Michigan published its October numbers.

Industry observers note that the year-over-year numbers show where Michigan’s growth comes from. Online sports betting AGR fell 3.3% from October 2025. For all of 2025, sportsbooks produced $435.9 million in AGR, while iGaming generated $3.1 billion in gross receipts. Online casino play therefore accounts for most of the state’s online gambling revenue.

Recent findings suggest that october sportsbook figures swung sharply from one month to the next. Sports betting AGR jumped 91.3% from September. Handle rose 11.1% to $605.4 million, and sportsbook gross receipts reached $70.7 million. Combined online casino and sports betting gross receipts totaled $388.8 million.

The broader online market had been growing faster earlier in the year. From January through July, combined online casino and sports betting AGR totaled $2.21 billion, up 20.9% from the same period in 2025. October’s casino growth is consistent with a market that is still expanding, but at a slower rate than a year ago.

Tribal online operators also made $8.9 million in payments to their governing bodies for October.

In a recent development, creating high-quality visual content once meant specialized cameras, technical knowledge and hours of editing. Today, software does a growing share of that work. Cameras recognize subjects, adjust exposure, stabilize footage and hand clips to editing tools that transcribe, reframe and tag them.

For developers and technical creators, the interesting part is how these features are built and where they fail. This article covers how computational photography prepared the ground, what on-device vision can and cannot do, how wearable cameras change capture, and how to add a small, tested quality check to your own media pipeline. It ends with the privacy and authenticity questions that come with building camera features. Product capabilities change quickly, so check each vendor's current documentation.

Sources indicate that digital photography made images easy to capture, review and share. Smartphones then folded capture, editing and publishing into one device. The next shift was computational photography: instead of relying only on the lens and sensor, the device combines several captures and processes them in software.

Sources indicate that high dynamic range (HDR) imaging is the clearest example. A camera captures frames at different exposures and merges them so both bright skies and dark foregrounds keep detail. Research indexed on PubMed, published in IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence, examines how deep learning has advanced HDR imaging, particularly in reconstructing visual information across different exposure levels.

Machine learning extends this approach from merging pixels to understanding them, which is what lets a camera decide what is the subject and what is the background.

Most AI camera features fall into a few groups.

In a recent development, these tools make real-time features practical, since a round trip to a server would add delay. They also keep raw frames on the user's device, which helps with the privacy concerns discussed below.

Because of these failure modes, a pipeline should check what the camera produced before running expensive downstream steps.

A cheap pre-check can reject a frame that is too soft or badly exposed before you spend time on transcription, upscaling or model inference. The script below uses numpy and Pillow. It measures sharpness as the variance of a Laplacian, a standard blur indicator, and measures exposure as the share of crushed and clipped pixels.

The test builds a detailed random frame and a blurred copy, then checks that the sharp frame scores far higher, that a mostly black frame is flagged as underexposed and that a mostly white frame is flagged as overexposed:.

Run the tests with python3 test_frame_quality.py. In our run, the detailed test frame scored about 33,000 for sharpness and its blurred copy scored under 2.

According to recent reports, traditional capture means holding a camera, propping up a phone or setting up equipment. Wearable cameras let creators record from their own point of view while their hands stay free, which suits travel video, instructional content, outdoor activities and behind-the-scenes footage.

Camera-equipped smart glasses are one form of this. Several makers sell them, and consumer listings such as ai glasses with camera show how the category is presented to buyers. Depending on the device, customers start recording with physical controls or voice commands. Specifications differ widely, so compare field of view, storage, battery life and software support before choosing one.

For developers, wearables change the input. Footage is shaky, framed by head movement and often recorded outdoors, which is exactly where a quality check and stabilization matter. Battery capacity, camera position, storage and recording duration also limit extended productions. Wearables are an additional option for perspectives that are hard to reach otherwise, not a replacement for traditional cameras.

Editing involves reviewing clips, correcting color, adjusting audio and preparing videos for each platform. AI tools automate several repetitive parts of that work:.

According to recent reports, creative judgment stays human. Choosing meaningful moments, shaping narrative flow and keeping a consistent visual style are decisions software cannot reliably make. Real-time assistance during recording will depend on hardware, software and environmental conditions.

Industry observers note that as cameras get smaller, responsible recording matters more. Wearable devices can capture footage without the obvious movements of a handheld camera, so people nearby may not know recording is happening. The European Data Protection Board has highlighted transparency, personal data protection and recording awareness as vital considerations for camera-equipped smart glasses.

It has been revealed that authenticity is the second challenge. AI tools can enhance an image, but heavy alteration can also mislead. The National Institute of Standards and Technology has examined technical approaches to digital content transparency, including provenance tracking, watermarking and synthetic-content detection. On the provenance side, the C2PA coalition publishes an open standard called Content Credentials, which helps show where content came from and what edits it has undergone.

Cameras will likely get better at faster subject recognition, more efficient automated editing and stronger low-light performance as computer vision and on-device computing advance. Wearables may widen first-person storytelling, and editing tools may make multi-platform publishing simpler. Technical gains alone will not decide quality, though. Originality, storytelling and thoughtful creative decisions still do.

According to recent reports, not always. Toolkits such as ML Kit face detection and Apple's Vision framework run image analysis on the device, which reduces delay and keeps frames local.

It narrows the gap in many conditions, but optics, sensor size and control still matter for demanding work, and AI enhancement can introduce artifacts of its own.

Add an early quality gate that checks sharpness and exposure, as in the script above, and calibrate its thresholds on your own footage.

Sources indicate that it depends on location and context. Regulators such as the European Data Protection Board have raised transparency and consent concerns, so check local rules and be open about recording.

Provenance standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to show a file's origin and edit history, though they only help when tools and platforms support them.

AI-powered cameras make photography and video production more accessible, efficient and flexible, from on-device subject recognition to automated editing and wearable capture. The same tools create new work for developers: checking output quality, handling their failure modes and building privacy and provenance into the product. Technology reduces technical barriers, but the creativity and judgment behind good content remain human.

Grabette: an open system to record robot-manipulation data

📅 21 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.
  • Industry observers note that robot learning has a supply problem.
  • It has been revealed that teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record your own manipulation tasks in minutes with a handheld gripper, turn them into robot-ready datasets automatically, and help grow an open, collaborative dataset for robot learning.

Industry observers note that robot learning has a supply problem. We have capable policy architectures (transformer-based VLAs, diffusion and flow-matching policies, and even world models) and the GPUs to train them. What we lack is large, diverse, real-world manipulation data.

It has been revealed that teleoperating a robot to collect it can be expensive and demanding: first of all, it requires a robot. And depending on the teleoperation method, data collection can be tedious for the user if it takes hours and involve significant hardware and logistical challenges. That is difficult to scale with the wide variety of tasks and environnements required.

Recent findings suggest that but you don't need a robot to collect robot data. Just a human hand, a gripper, a camera, and a way to recover the 6-DoF trajectory of what the hand did. Capture the demonstration and you have data a robot can learn from.

It has been revealed that that's what we're releasing today: Grabette, an open, low-cost system for recording manipulation data. Pick it up, record a task with your own hand, and get back a clean, robot-ready dataset. No robot, no lab, no teleop rig.

And that's the bigger goal: if recording a demonstration is as easy as shooting a video, anyone can contribute. We want Grabette to seed a large, open, collaborative manipulation dataset. One no single lab could ever build alone.

Grabette is directly inspired by the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) from Stanford: a handheld gripper with a fisheye camera that records demonstrations "in the wild", recovers camera trajectories with SLAM, and trains visuomotor policies from them.

In a recent development, UMI proved the recipe works. Other (closed source) devices exists like Agibot's MEgo gripper, Genrobot's DAS gripper and Sunday Robotics skill capture glove. Our goal was to make it effortless to use, to get the barrier from "I have a task" to "I have a trained model" as low as possible.

Recent findings suggest that grabette is built into the modern open ecosystem: LeRobot for datasets, the Hugging Face Hub for sharing, and a processing pipeline you run from your browser with nothing to install. Grabette is something anyone can build on a workbench, use in the field, and contribute data from.

It has been revealed that we have been developing Grabette for months, and we feel it has become usable enough to share. We are excited to share it now with you!

Grabette is a handheld gripper instrumented with everything needed to reconstruct a manipulation demonstration.

It carries two cameras, each with a distinct job. Splitting the two roles is deliberate: the cheap wide fisheye gives the policy the context-rich, wrist-camera-style view it needs, while the RGBD camera does the heavy lifting of robust 6-DoF tracking.

And while Grabette records data during tasks performed by a user, it relies on its robotic counterpart to execute the movements it has learned after training. So, meet Gripette, the robotic arm end-effector twin of Grabette.

The family shares the same hardware DNA:.

Grabette hand held recording device (left) and Gripette robot gripper (right).

It has been revealed that components. Standard sensors you can buy, no closed pipeline, no fork lock-in. A Raspberry Pi, a standard Pi camera, an off-the-shelf OAK-D depth camera, magnetic encoders. The whole point is that anyone can build one from parts you can just order.

It has been revealed that robot-agnostic by design. Nothing in the capture or the data format assumes a particular arm. Demonstrations are stored as camera-local 6-DoF cartesian pose plus gripper state, the output is a standard LeRobot dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, so the same data can drive different robots and different learning methods. You will still need the matching Gripette gripper on your arm though.

This release enables anyone to go from "I want to demonstrate a task" to "I have a training-ready dataset" quickly and without prior expertise.

Press the button, and data from the observation camera, the tracking camera (color, depth, and IMU), and the gripper’s encoder joint values are recorded simultaneously, using a single shared clock to ensure proper synchronization. Press the button again to stop the episode, and the data is saved locally on the Raspberry Pi.

Open the Grabette dashboard in your browser. Select the episodes you want to add to the dataset, and with one click, post-processing begins.

Everything is now ready to start training!

It has been revealed that A dataset is only interesting if it trains something. So, to show the loop end-to-end, we ship a complete example. But to be clear, this is an example of what is enables, not the product: the release is the recording system. Your Grabette data works with any method that consumes LeRobot datasets.

Our example takes 200 recorded demonstrations such as :.

Dataset available on this HF Dataset.

Policy available on this HF Model.

The data bottleneck doesn’t get solved by one lab, but by a community recording demonstrations everywhere. You can now help build the dataset: build a Grabette, record tasks you are interested in, and share them on the Hub. Every episode makes the open dataset bigger and more diverse, and every contributor makes robot learning a little less gated behind expensive hardware.

Recent findings suggest that this release is only the start of the project! Grabette will keep evolving. We already have more coming, including Casquette, a head-mounted POV device to complement Grabette for egocentric capture (still a work in progress). But the most vital next step isn’t only ours, it’s also yours: start recording, and let’s build the dataset together.

CSS-Tricks, Version 20

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks.
  • Industry observers note that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time.
  • Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’ve been bashing on updating this site’s design for the last couple of weeks. It’s high time things get a fresh coat of paint, right? The last version of CSS-Tricks was pushed five years ago. That’s ancient in web (and dog) years.

Industry observers note that it’s not like the site has simply sat all that time. We pushed lots of changes and shipped upcoming features, particularly since 2024, but we never really got the paint brushes out of storage.

Now, before there’s a chorus of “things don’t look thaaaat different” I want to say I’m rarely a fan of complete re-builds and tend to lean into iterative releases. And the upcoming v20 theme is what I’d call an iterative rollup that’s worthy of a version bump.

Let’s go over the most notable updates to see why.

It has been revealed that first and foremost, some of the biggest changes are what you don’t see. As you might imagine, this site has carried over plenty of pieces across 19 years. I decided to excavate the theme and definitely found some ghosts to bust.

According to recent reports, for example, the global compiled JavaScript file retained some scripts that just weren’t being used anymore. Things like handling embedded versions of the newsletter from before we began self-hosting the posts. There were relics that catered specifically to the Flexbox Guide for handling toggles back before we had proper HTML . There was a jQuery lazy-loader thing that is well-covered by WordPress core now. We had some scripts for serving third-party ads that are no longer needed now that we’re self-hosting ads. Things like that. The overall JavaScript was nicely trimmed from 151.6 KB (55.3 KB gzipped) to 133.8 KB (48.1 KB).

I also decided to formally retire the CSS-Tricks Forum. We put it in “archive mode” back in, like, 2018. None of those discussions are particularly valuable for today as they were over 10 years ago, so I deactivated the bbPress plugin that powered it and cleared out the database… and wow, that carved a whopping 400 MB from the ol’ database, not to mention it allowed me to drop several custom templates from the theme.

There were more ghosts busted along the way and, to be sure, there are still some lurking around. But it’s way less scary poking around the theme directory now, and further cleanup should be a lot easier from here on out.

Yeah, yeah, raise your hand if you’re still running Gulp. We are 🙋‍♂️. That’s not a bad thing in and of itself, but keeping it in a fixed state for all this time is not the greatest. I think we’re sporting a more modern workflow than before, even if there’s still room to grow. A smattering of the related commits:.

According to recent reports, for years, I endured the same errors every time I fired up a newly introduced terminal. Those are gone and things run super cleanly, not to mention quickly. Very happy here.

Sources indicate that oof, this is everyone’s favorite job, right?! Aside from being able to spot and fix a few unescaped custom field calls here and there, I decided to ask Claude to help me with a holistic audit. I prompted it to review recent WordPress security release notes and identify areas where the theme could be hardened to comply with what WordPress is doing.

Industry observers note that whoa, you used AI? Yeah, I sure did. But for things like this where it could be my little gopher and allow me more time to do what I do best: front-end. I’m still able to make most of the patches myself based on the output recommendations, but it’s nice to have a gut-check for things where I’m clearly no expert, like security.

Recent findings suggest that I still use and like Sass very much. I mean, yes, I would like to be straight-up vanilla CSS everywhere, but I can’t tear myself away from partials in particular.

Recent findings suggest that the previous theme had a fairly nice “flat” structure — very few partial directories and most things all in the same top-level source. Totally cool. But an organization nut like me (you should see my house) has to have a place for everything to live. It ain’t perfect, but I’m happy with what I was able to put together without leveling the building in the process.

Sources indicate that there are some compromises. Like, /header should really be in /layout. The ordering is really important, though, and some of my ideals were simply not possible. I’m hoping to eventually work in some sort of Cascade Layers structure.

It has been revealed that I’m pleased as punch to see the overall size of CSS drop in the process. It went from 180 KB (31.7 KB) to 169 KB (24.6 KB). Not hugely significant, but not not significant either. I had to do a couple tricky things to cheat my way there, like serving all the form styles I’m about to talk about into a separate forms.css file and serving it just on pages where WooCommerce, Restrict Content Pro, and Gravity Forms are enqueued.

Industry observers note that are you starting to notice a trend? We’re still talking about fairly invisible work. CSS-Tricks has so many nooks and crannies that it’s nearly impossible to make things perfectly consistent across the board. But because of those nooks and crannies, so many fixed values, magic numbers, one-off styles, and older utilities were hiding about. I decided to tackle a good chunk of that while reorganizing the Sass.

Recent findings suggest that for example, there are now semantic design tokens that abstract away one-off colors. So many grays, let me tell you. Now there’s a maintainable palette that’s referenced throughout. Same with fonts, font styles, and font sizes. Same with paddings and margins. It feels a lot better to make a change at the “system” level with confidence that the change is taking effect everywhere it needs to.

According to recent reports, but this is also where some clearly visible changes happened! Most notably, link styles are consistent all over the place with a small handful of intended and maintained variations. Not only is it more pleasing visually, but it improves accessibility throughout because the inherited styles default to proper visual cues that do not rely solely on color or opacity changes.

Oh, and my favorite piece of this? Forms and tables have both been redone. That’s tough to do in a WordPress theme where these components don’t always come from one source. For example, forms could come from any one of the Gravity Forms, WooCommerce, or Restrict Content Pro plugins, and they all have their own stylesheets. Resetting those allowed me to bring a certain level of harmony in all those instances.

OK, something even more visual. This is the first time CSS-Tricks has had more than one color scheme! It certainly could have been done a long time ago, but I’d also argue that the design hasn’t really called for a light/dark toggle over the last 8 years or so. It’s a nice blend of both light and dark elements that marry the best of both worlds no matter your theme preference.

Recent findings suggest that but I had to take a stab, right? The site has predominantly been dark despite the content being against a white background, so I treated things as though a “dark” mode already existed. The result is a creamy light theme that is largely just a change in background and component styles. And I used some of what I learned from the recent “toggle” debate to handle system, dark, and light themes with a single toggle.

Sources indicate that what hasn’t changed is the main content container you see in things like articles. That was already white, even in a “dark” mode, and I’m not confident that simply toggling it between white and black is the best approach. Something on the radar for sure.

Oh, and it’s all wired up to a view transition that slides the new theme over the previous one.

I hope you think the site’s header and footer are cute. Yes, cute. That’s what I was going for when adding a colorful series of dots as the backdrop.

According to recent reports, sorta like a subtle candy texture, right? Or a colorful group of stars? I dunno, but I’m calling it “Jawbreaker” for lack of a better term and because it reminds me of the jawbreaker candy I loved as a kid. Naming still sucks.

In a recent development, it’s all part of the same SVG. I really, really (really) wanted to random()-ly position dots around, but that would have taken a lot of empty individual elements (e.g., ) in the markup. Not my favorite. So, I generate the elements in PHP:.

I really, really wanted to random()-ize all the things, but inlining random coordinates on each was the way to go. Same deal with the inlined styles that set a fill, and sizing for each circle in the texture, and variables that set a --delay and --dur on the subtle animation that twinkles them in and out.

I’ll have to look at generating the SVG using or whatever later since that pattern repeats in the footer, too.

That’s carried through to the 404 page as well:.

Industry observers note that if your browser supports border-shape and random() (only Chrome, I think), then the homepage gives you a blobby-blob shape behind the grid of author avatars. Hover it and it gets, you know, even blobbier.

It takes an existing pattern I’m calling .gradient-card:.

…and sets a gradient on the component’s :before pseudo:.

That sits underneath the :after pseudo that’s translucent, allowing the :before‘s gradient to show through a smidge:.

The differing border-radius values allow :before to bleed outside, giving the impression of a border around the entire deal. That’s the basic shape. The border-shape is where things get blobby:.

Those variables? They’re mapped to shape()s. I grabbed the first one from Temani Afif’s blob generator:.

It’s called “static” because that’s the default state. Hover or focus on the component and it swaps out those points out with a “hover” version of the shape:.

It has been revealed that those variables? They’re mapped to random() values:.

It has been revealed that so, the hover state is different on each page load. And we animate between the two:.

I’m pretty stoked on this one. The Almanac has grown, evolved, and just plain gotten great the past few years. But the primary page for it… not so great. It was definitely overshadowed by work on the pages inside it and never revisited beyond clickable cards to get to each feature subset.

Industry observers note that now the page is a real index of the CSS features that gets you where you need to go promptly. Someone somewhere sometime did some sort of CSS periodic table. I forget where I’d seen that but the general idea sat with me and I thought I could pull it off. There’s nothing “tricky” about it but I love what the layout adds to the overall site.

This is another area that sorely needed love. Our guides have always been a vertical stack of items. The book effect was definitely cool, but I started believing that leaning on it as the main visual hook was holding things back from being more functional. With something like 27 guides, we’re talking about a lot of scrolling with no clear idea of what you’re going to see as you go.

According to recent reports, again, nothing “tricky” but I like the overall usefulness of the latest layout. There’s a featured guide, a widget of newly added and updated guides, and a categorized grid of everything below that.

The pages that show all of an author’s published articles got a little spruce-up, too.

Sources indicate that it’s a little change, really. The right sidebar was moved to the left and the author image and bio moved in, allowing the articles to creep up to the top. I hope to do more here since the small layout tweak opens up more opportunities.

Also need to do the larger Authors index, but another time.

Industry observers note that this one’s just for those of us working in the WordPress editor. I don’t need a complete visual editor to get things done, but it is a nice affordance to have some of the front-end styles sneak into the editing UI for a better idea of what you’re working with.

Recent findings suggest that using Lighthouse to measure things like performance, accessibility, and best practices is woefully fraught with caveats, but there’s no reason to chuck it completely. I find them more fun than fact and I don’t mind the recommendations for improving things.

So, after a few runs and tweaks, here’s how things shook out theme-to-theme.

In a recent development, I’m happy here. There are some things I just don’t have the control to fix when it comes to performance, so seeing v20 come in consistent with v19 is just fine by me. I’m happier with the boosts to accessibility and best practices. SEO? Meh. Don’t really care unless it’s hurting more vital things like accessibility.

Again, very happy. There’s little I can do with time to first byte but everything else seems to clock in at least marginally better. The total page weight is a clear win and that’s probably what I care most about here.

In a recent development, oh gosh, there’s a lot more but they’re mostly minor things that don’t bubble up to the front end. Sort of the same way browser changelogs have some generic line of “bug squashing” or whatever. In this case, it’s things like better post queries and breadcrumbs and function management and naming and… you get it.

In a recent development, there’s definitely so much more to do. And plenty of things I’m sure I missed or broke along the way. That’s just life and those will have to come in another iterative release less worthy of a version bump. You can let me know what I muffed up in the comments.

I hope you at least like where this is going!

  • In a recent development, utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, utah has sued the companies behind the Stake sweepstakes site, alleging it ran an illegal casino for Utahns since 2022. The case follows Florida's own suit against Stake and adds to the legal pressure on the dual-currency sweepstakes model.

The timing of Utah’s suit against Stake stands out. Stake added Utah to its list of restricted states on Nov. 13, four days before the suit was filed, yet state consumer protection investigators could still use the site as recently as Nov. 16, when a banner said access would end on Dec. 7, the 43-page complaint claims.

In a recent development, utah Attorney General Derek Brown and the Utah Department of Commerce’s Division of Consumer Protection brought the case. It names two defendants: Sweepsteaks Limited, based in Cyprus, and its Australian parent, Easygo Group Holdings Pty Ltd. The state refers to them jointly as Stake.

The central allegation is that Stake has offered Utahns a round-the-clock casino since 2022. Utah has prohibited gambling since it became a state, and its Constitution bans gambling.

According to recent reports, the complaint takes aim at how the site works. Players spend real money on two virtual currencies.

In a recent development, utah wants the court to declare the site illegal gambling under state law. It also asks the court to bar Stake from offering its games in Utah and to order the company to return money taken from residents. The state is also seeking fines under the Utah Consumer Sales Practices Act and a remedy for harm to the public. The complaint adds claims for unjust enrichment, public nuisance and declaratory judgment.

Sources indicate that A demand that players’ losses be repaid raises the stakes for the wider industry. Taken together, the relief Utah seeks increases the legal risk for sweepstakes operators, suppliers and affiliates nationwide.

Utah is not the only state to bring Stake itself into court. Florida’s suit is broader in scope. It names Sweepsteaks Ltd and Easygo alongside Medium Rare and Kick Streaming, NEXT.io reported. It also names co-founders Bijan Tehrani and Ed Craven, plus payment firms Praxis and Breeze Labs Payments. Utah’s complaint is limited to the two corporate defendants.

Other states have targeted the same business model through a different operator. Kentucky and Arkansas have both sued VGW, which runs its own dual-currency sweepstakes sites.

The Stake case is separate from Utah’s clash with federal regulators over prediction markets. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has sued Utah to stop the state from using its own laws to shut down CFTC-registered contract markets. The Stake suit also came less than three weeks after Utah filed criminal charges against Kalshi’s founders. Those charges include felony counts of online gambling promotion.

Court records did not list a lawyer for either defendant, and the firm did not answer a request for comment on the suit.

CSS Optimization: Is Using Declarations Just Once (UDJO) Still Effective Today?
