Quantization-Aware Healing: a compressed, 4-bit model that outperforms its full-precision original

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2500 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost.
  • Recent findings suggest that our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it?
  • Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

Recent findings suggest that our latest paper, Quantization-Aware Healing: A Practical Recipe for Recovering Compressed, 4-Bit LLMs, asks a question that the field has mostly left open: once a model has already been through structural compression, not just quantization, how well does that recovery step actually work, and what is the right way to do it? We introduce Quantization-Aware Healing (QAH), and applied to a GPT-OSS 120B model compressed to 60B parameters and quantized to MXFP4, it produces a model that beats its own full-precision (bfloat16) version on 7 of 9 benchmarks. The 4-bit model ends up smaller, cheaper to run, and more accurate than the checkpoint it was quantized from. This inverts the usual relationship between a 4-bit model and the 16-bit model it came from.

Most efficiency pipelines follow the same three steps: compress the architecture, quantize the compressed weights, then heal the damage. The difference between methods is entirely in that last step.

It has been revealed that the dominant healing recipe is quantization-aware training (QAT). It inserts fake-quantization operators into the forward pass and keeps fine-tuning the model on a task loss, so the weights learn to tolerate the low-precision representation. In practice this means re-running an already expensive multi-stage post-training process, supervised fine-tuning, RLHF, agentic tuning, through a noisier, lower-precision forward pass. It is costly, and as our results show, it can also become unstable if training continues too long past its best point.

According to recent reports, an alternative, quantization-aware distillation (QAD), avoids re-running that history. Instead of a task loss, it distills a frozen full-precision teacher directly into the quantized student through a KL-divergence loss on the output logits. This works well when the only change is quantization, because a genuine full-precision version of the exact same model exists to act as teacher. But once a model has gone through structural compression, fewer layers, heads, or neurons, and not just fewer bits, that assumption breaks. There is no independently trained full-precision version of the smaller architecture. The only candidate teacher is the recovered bfloat16 checkpoint, which is itself a distilled approximation of the original model. Distilling from it anchors the quantized student to a degraded target and caps its accuracy at that recovered checkpoint's own ceiling.

So the question of how to heal a model that has been both structurally compressed and quantized was, until now, genuinely open.

QAH removes that ceiling with one change: it distills directly from the original, pre-compression model rather than from the recovered one. Teacher and student do not even share an architecture. The teacher is full-size and full-precision, the student is half the size and running in MXFP4. Because a teacher's output distribution is architecture-agnostic, nothing about the size or shape mismatch prevents the transfer. The student never sees hard labels, only the teacher's output distribution, matched through KL divergence on the logits.

In a recent development, this reframes what the quantization stage is doing. Under QAH it is no longer a lossy postprocessing step applied after healing is finished. It is a second, full pass of distillation against the original teacher, supervision that the bfloat16 checkpoint never received. The 4-bit student is not compensating for information lost to quantization; it is picking up information the earlier recovery stage did not have the time or data to transfer.

It has been revealed that there is also a stability benefit that falls out of the loss itself. Because KL distillation ties the student to a fixed teacher distribution, once the student catches up there is no further pressure for it to drift. A cross-entropy task loss, by contrast, keeps pushing the student toward hard labels indefinitely. That difference turns out to matter for both accuracy and training stability, as the comparison below reveals.

It has been revealed that to make QAH work at long context, where the healing corpus includes documents up to 32k tokens, we reuse the memory-efficient chunked KL-divergence loss from our companion paper on efficient distillation. That loss computes the KL one slice of the sequence at a time and never materializes the full vocabulary-by-sequence grid, which is what makes 32k-token healing fit inside a fixed GPU memory budget. We covered the mechanics of that loss in a previous post.

QAH overview. After structural compression and quantization, capabilities drop sharply. QAH distills from the original model, a frozen teacher whose logits are precomputed offline, rather than from the recovered checkpoint. Source: paper Figure 1.

In a recent development, we applied QAH to a GPT-OSS 120B model, compressed to 60B parameters and recovered in bfloat16, then re-quantized to MXFP4 under QAH. The natural comparison is against that same 60B model's bfloat16 checkpoint, the best full-precision version of this architecture that exists. The QAH model wins on 7 of the 9 benchmarks.

The two benchmarks where QAH trails, MMLU-Pro and SciCode, lose by less than a point and a half. Everywhere else the 4-bit model is ahead of its own 16-bit source, and the largest gains land on exactly the capabilities compression usually damages most: long-context reasoning (+7.4 on AA-LCR) and math (+5.6 on AIME 2025).

The comparison against the original 120B teacher is just as telling. Despite running at half the teacher's parameter count and roughly a quarter of its weight memory, the QAH model surpasses the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench (66.5 vs. 66.0) and comes within 1.6 points on GPQA Diamond (67.4 vs. 69.0). The largest remaining gap against the teacher is on AA-LCR, an extreme long-context benchmark where the capacity lost to compression is intrinsically the hardest to recover.

Industry observers note that the 4-bit QAH model matches or beats its bfloat16 source on 7 of 9 benchmarks, and beats the full-size teacher on LiveCodeBench. Source: paper Figure 2.

To isolate the effect of the loss function from everything else, we also compared QAH directly against QAT under matched conditions, quantizing a GPT-OSS 9B model to MXFP4 and tracking average performance across MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA Diamond as training progresses.

Both methods reach a similar peak, 54.9 for QAH against 54.6 for QAT, so on best-case accuracy they are effectively tied. The difference is in how they get there and what happens afterwards. QAH reaches its peak in about 100 steps, roughly 7 times faster than QAT's 700, and then stays within about two points of that peak for the rest of training. QAT collapses sharply once past its peak, shedding nearly 19 points by step 1,200.

Sources indicate that the practical consequence is a real deployment risk difference. A QAT checkpoint needs careful early stopping against a held-out signal to avoid shipping a model that has already started to degrade, whereas a sufficiently trained QAH checkpoint can be served safely because it simply does not drift. This is consistent with the mechanism: KL distillation against a frozen teacher gives the student no incentive to move once it matches the teacher, while a cross-entropy objective keeps pushing on hard labels and eventually erodes capabilities the model inherited from the original.

According to recent reports, QAH peaks at 54.9 in roughly 100 steps and holds; QAT reaches 54.6 only around step 700, then loses nearly 19 points by step 1,200. Source: paper Figure 3.

Recent findings suggest that the accuracy story comes paired with the efficiency story that motivated compression in the first place. At 4-bit precision the QAH model uses roughly 4 times less weight memory than the bfloat16 student, and at half the parameter count of the 120B teacher it roughly halves compute per token, which is what lets it run on substantially smaller hardware. For model families that ship in bfloat16 rather than 4-bit, the combined parameter and precision reduction would be closer to 8 times less compute per token.

In a recent development, the takeaway is that a compressed, 4-bit model does not have to be a lower-accuracy version of its full-precision counterpart. With this healing recipe it can be smaller, cheaper to serve, and more accurate at the same time, and it reaches that point in a fraction of the training a QAT recipe would need. Quantization stops being a tax you pay for efficiency and becomes an extra opportunity to teach the model.

Sources indicate that this work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making large models smaller and cheaper to run without giving up the capabilities that make them useful. It sits alongside our companion work on efficient distillation, which supplies the long-context training machinery QAH depends on.

Want the full technical details, including the healing pipeline, the chunked KL implementation for long-context healing, and the distributed-training findings? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying compression and healing to your own models.

It has been revealed that making a large language model smaller almost always comes with a cost. The now-standard recipe for efficient deployment is to compress the architecture first, cutting the parameter count by removing layers, heads, or neurons, and then quantize the remaining weights down to 4 bits to shrink memory and compute further. Both steps save a lot, but together they systematically degrade the capabilities people actually care about: reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, and code generation. Because of this, serious deployment pipelines add a recovery step, usually called healing, before the model goes into production. Recent open-weight releases such as rbtv77 gpt-oss, NVIDIA's Nemotron family, and our own Hypernova 60B all rely on some version of this compress-then-heal approach.

This is a really fascinating take on model compression 🤯🔥. The idea that a 4-bit model can actually outperform the full-precision version turns the usual assumption about quantization completely upside down.... Instead of simply accepting the accuracy loss that comes with compression, QAH seems to show how targeted recovery can bring back—and even improve—important capabilities like reasoning, math, and coding. 🧠⚡.

What really caught my attention is the result with the compressed GPT-OSS 120B → 60B model.... Getting a smaller MXFP4 model to beat its own bfloat16 checkpoint on 7 of 9 benchmarks is pretty impressive. 📊🚀 It makes the whole compress-then-heal pipeline feel much more practical for real-world deployment, especially when memory usage and inference costs matter.

Recent findings suggest that I also like the broader implication here.... Quantization doesn't necessarily have to mean sacrificing model quality if the recovery process is designed with the quantized model in mind. 💡🔧 A smaller model that costs less to operate while still delivering stronger benchmark performance could be a huge advantage for teams trying to deploy capable LLMs efficiently.

It has been revealed that definitely an interesting direction for efficient AI deployment.... Turning a heavily compressed 4-bit model into something that can outperform its larger full-precision counterpart is the kind of result that makes you rethink what "compression" actually means. 👏🔥 Really curious to see how far Quantization-Aware Healing can go across other architectures and workloads.... 🚀🧠.

Hi there! From how I'm reading this, I think you might have missed a method error in your experiment that invalidates your headline.

Industry observers note that the headline comparison looks like it has no control. The bf16 60B got one round of distillation and the MXFP4 60B got that round plus a second round from a better teacher. The obvious missing comparison is to give the bf16 60B the identical second distillation pass in bf16, same data, same steps, same teacher. Without that comparison you cannot separate "QAH is a good recipe" from "we trained one checkpoint longer against a teacher than the other.".

In a recent development, results table labels the teacher "120B teacher (MXFP4)", which is right since gpt-oss-120b ships with MXFP4 MoE weights natively. But the approach section indicates the teacher is full-size and full-precision, and the title claims the student beats its full-precision original. Those contradict.

Unless I'm wrong, I'd retract this and consdier republishing when you can show the significant difference on the comparable arms without extending one further than the other with more compute.

Recent findings suggest that you're right that the headline table compares checkpoints with unequal training. The 60B bf16 checkpoint got one distillation pass (the recovery); the 60B MXFP4 checkpoint got that pass plus a second one against the 120B teacher. We describe that second pass in the approach section, but we should have been explicit that the table therefore doesn't, on its own, separate "distilling under quantization" from "distilling for longer." We'll add that caveat to the text.

A bit of context on what the paper is: it's an applied case study, not a theoretical claim. The question we set out to answer is the one a deployment team faces: Given a compressed model that has to ship in 4 bits, what's the best way to run the quantization step? The result we stand behind is narrow and reproducible: the shipped 4-bit checkpoint scores above the bf16 checkpoint it was quantized from, rather than below it, which is the usual outcome of direct post-training quantization. What we shouldn't have leaned into is the stronger causal reading, that quantization itself is "free training", and you're right that the current table doesn't isolate that.

In a recent development, the comparison that would settle it is the one you describe: the bf16 60B given the identical second pass. same data, steps, teacher and, separately, that continued bf16 checkpoint post-training-quantized to MXFP4. The second is really the decision anyone deploying faces: heal under quantization, or quantize afterwards. If we extend this for a revised version, those are the arms we'd add; either way we're flagging them as a limitation of the current version rather than claiming the table resolves the question.

We don't think retraction is the right call. The reported numbers are real and reproducible, and the practical result stands. But we agree the causal framing needs that control, and we'd rather correct it in the open than argue it. Appreciate the push.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.
  • The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Still slinging hardware – now with added AI and attendant risks or opportunities.

Dell and HPE this week both told investors they’ve become “different companies.”.

The two hardware giants made that assertion on their respective earnings calls this week. HPE went first, on Monday, when CEO Antonio Neri declared “We are now a fundamentally different manufacturer” after acquiring Juniper Networks and creating products “built to capitalize on the next phase of AI.”.

On Tuesday, Dell’s chief operating officer and vice chairman Jeff Clarke declared “We are now a different company” because the Infrastructure Solutions Group (ISG) has become the source of “the vast majority of our profit and growth.”.

HPE’s claim to having changed is perhaps more credible on the face of it, given that its acquisition of Juniper means it has become more of a networking player.

Dell hasn’t made significant additions to its hardware portfolio, but there’s a big difference in its sources of revenue, which three years ago was just about evenly split between its infrastructure and client devices. In its Tuesday announcement, Dell revealed ISG revenue grew 198 percent year over year to $42 billion, while CSG racked up three percent growth to $12.9 billion – meaning Dell is now predominantly an infrastructure company.

Clarke noted he’s seen some companies deferring their PC purchases to buy AI hardware instead, and said Dell is re-assigning parts it ordered to build PCs and using them for servers instead.

According to recent reports, dell exited its Q3 with a backlog of $32 billion worth of AI servers and is clearly aware that investors might worry that’s not a useful metric because some buyers’ dreams of operating neoclouds have struck financial or regulatory barriers. Clarke assured investors that Dell is “highly selective about the partners we work with”.

“Every AI order is vetted for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance, and access to land and power.”.

It has been revealed that HPE also has wrinkles in its AI business, because buyers won’t stand for fat margins and that’s dented the company’s profits a little. Neri was able to point to AI-related revenue also rising sharply, up 68.6 percent year over year to $11.3 billion, while overall revenue climbed 50 percent to reach $14.5 billion. Networking grew at a more relaxed 12 percent.

The CEO remarked HPE expects better growth ahead, because latest server purchases create demand for networks and storage. He also pointed to HPE having the opportunity to sell its networking kit to other OEMs who build AMD’s Helios rack-scale systems. HPE predicted its next quarter will see revenue reach $14.0 billion to $14.6 billion, up 51 to 57 percent year over year.

Recent findings suggest that dell is also optimistic that AI buyers will spend on kit beyond servers and GPUs and updated its full-year revenue outlook to $202 billion, $10 billion above its previous forecasts and up 78 percent year over year. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning.
  • Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me.
  • In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rust has a curious feature that I don’t think the language would land today, if it was not there for a long time: mutex poisoning. When some Rust code panics while holding a std::sync::Mutex, the mutex is poisoned. That means that any further call to lock() returns a PoisonError. The motivation for this feature is that an object might have some internal invariants that need to be upheld and panicking in the wrong moment might invalidate reasonable at and leave an object behind in a broken state.

Personally I absolutely hate this feature as it has bitten me so many times and I cannot once remember it helping me. The libs team is discussing making the non-poisoning locks the default in the next edition but entirely expectedly it has caused quite a few people to jump to the defence of the feature.

In this post I want to make my personal case why poisoned locks should either be entirely removed or be made the exception.

Industry observers note that primarily this is because I have yet to come across code in the wild that handles a poisoned lock correctly. On the other hand I have come across enough code that mishandles it and as a result behaves worse than a parking_lot lock would which does not support poisoning.

Josh Triplett put it quite strongly in a hackernews comment: “In the entire history of the standard library, we have never once seen a single report of anyone attempting to recover from poison.”.

In a recent development, when a panic happens with a lock held, there are two reasonable reactions: shut the process down, or carry on and ignore the flag. With panic = "abort" you get the former and poisoning never comes up. From all the evidence I have seen, with unwinding, the idiomatic lock().unwrap() picks the worst option of all.

Industry observers note that that’s because it neither stops the process nor lets it continue as it will turn every further lock into a panic with sometimes disastrous effects. But that is not the only glitch with the system today. So here I want to share some of the issues and with some references to real world code of how people got bitten.

According to recent reports, one subtle aspect to the poisoning is that the PoisonError needs to hold the guard. That’s because in order to ignore the poison flag, you need to fetch the guard from the error object. Holding on to the error means holding on to the lock!

That can cause common code that does error wrapping / error conversions into a deadlock hazard. The innocent looking m.lock()? in a function returning Box or similar keeps the mutex locked for as long as the error lives (#159930).

This can also happen with if let. For instance in cc-switch you can see that they had a test hung because a if let Ok(..) = lock() { .. } else { .. } fallback locked the same mutex again while the unnamed PoisonError from the condition still owned the guard. PC-AI had the same bug in a match arm. Another case can be found in ox-embed-server.

Sources indicate that deviously poisoning does not fail fast and done wrong, it fails forever. The original panic happens once, on one thread, often somewhere unrelated from future failures. Every later lock().unwrap() on that lock now however panics as well, and because so much Rust code survives panics (thread pools, request handlers, tokio tasks, FFI boundaries), the process stays up and becomes useless:.

While not live services, test suites show the same general issue. One failing test poisons a shared static and every test after it fails with PoisonError. This problem demonstrated up for cargo, deno, polars and rustc itself.

If you recover with into_inner(), the flag stays set and every later access takes the recovery path again. And remember that for the first nine years of Rust after the poisoning feature landed, you could not even clear it as clear_poison arrived only in 1.77. Not clearing the flag means that potentially expensive side effects will happen from that point onwards:.

goose-in-a-pond rebuilt its decoder state on every transcription after a single panic, librefang logged the same warning on every access, and a pool threw its model away on every return.

Recent findings suggest that so who is handling poisonings? I’m really not sure, definitely not the standard library. Every place where the standard library’s own code ignores it. Standard I/O has done so since March 2015, two months before 1.0, because “any poison must have been the result of user code which the lock isn’t protecting”. A common issue with a lot of poisoning errors that never had anything to do with the mutex that was held.

Recent findings suggest that same with the panic output capture, the backtrace lock and the WASI environment lock. They all do the same and unsurprisingly there is an open PR to move std’s internal mutexes to nonpoison.

And I would argue the ecosystem has largely come to the same conclusion. Tokio’s own locks don’t poison. Internally it wraps the std one in an adapter that removes poison. When it landed Carl Lerche remarked “I rather pretend lock poisoning isn’t a thing.” In one case Eliza Weisman needed into_inner to unlink a waiter during drop, or “we’ll leave the list with a potentially dangling pointer”. I want to point to this in particular because this is a case where poisoning stood in the way of memory safety which is commonly argued as a reason you want poisoning.

Another aspect here is why this is done on Mutex but not on RefCell. Surely if the case for poisoning is that some code temporarily breaks an invariant, panics, and someone else observes the broken state, then this should apply to more cases.

Take the usual example that argues in favor of poisoning and replace Mutex with RefCell, and you have exactly the same problem. Threads are not needed at all and this is not hypothetical either as tokio catches every task panic. Paired with a LocalSet the panic comes back as a JoinError, the next borrow() succeeds and reads a null pointer exactly like the mutex example from the problem.

Given how much panic catching goes on in async code, much of which is !Send for performance reasons, I’m not even convinced that panics get caught more often in multi-threaded code yet nobody asks for RefCell to poison.

The standard library isn’t consistent with itself either as LazyLock poisons for good, OnceLock never poisons, Mutex poisons but lets you recover.

Also remember that poisoning only tracks panics and a more common early return has the same glitch. The ? operator (as well as the try! macro before) that returns early from the middle of a critical section leaves the same broken invariant behind an unpoisoned lock.

Note also that the coupling of poisoning of mutexes is historical and an explicit Poison type would allow you to opt into this for any interior mutability wrapper.

Personally I hope the rust team stabilizes std::sync::nonpoison, have std::sync::Mutex resolve to it by default. If someone wants poisoning add that separate Poison wrapper then anyone who believes they need and can handle it, can opt into it for any type including RefCell or tokio threads.

Industry observers note that what I think would be the worst of all outcomes is the counter-proposal is to keep poisoning but have lock() panic instead of returning a Result. That would only fix the held guard lock semantics, and to a smaller degree the ergonomics, but it makes the slow outage the only option. That is what every lock().unwrap() does today, and the challenges above should be plenty of evidence of this being a problematic behavior in light of the existence of catch_unwind.

The post In defense of lock poisoning is the best argument for the other side and worth reading but I believe the evidence all points the other way, and most of what Oxide ships aborts on panic anyway which is also a reasonable behavior.

Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

In a recent development, from there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Sources indicate that let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

Industry observers note that I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

In a recent development, using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

Sources indicate that when it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

In a recent development, how we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an problem in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

Recent findings suggest that one group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

According to recent reports, now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Sources indicate that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

Tech Report: Granite 4.2 LLMs: How They're Built

📅 25 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B.
  • According to recent reports, granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technical walkthrough of how we built the Granite 4.2 reasoning model family.

It has been revealed that TL;DR: Granite 4.2 is our first family of dense, decoder-only reasoning LLMs, released in three sizes: 3B, 8B, and 30B. These models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were pre-trained from scratch on roughly 15T tokens with a five-phase strategy that extends the context window to 512K tokens, supervised fine-tuned on chain-of-thought, reasoning, and agentic-trajectory data, then post-trained with a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline. That pipeline includes agentic RL, where the 8B and 30B models learn to act with tools inside real sandboxed environments. Every model has a thinking / non-thinking switch, a low-effort thinking mode that spends a short reasoning budget on easy questions, and native tool calling. All Granite 4.2 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

According to recent reports, granite 4.2 is the reasoning-focused release of the Granite language-model family. Earlier Granite releases were strong instruction-following assistants; Granite 4.2 adds explicit reasoning. Every model can produce a chain of thought before its answer and can run in thinking or non-thinking mode depending on how much deliberation a task needs. A low-effort mode falls between the two, spending a short reasoning budget on easy questions.

The three sizes (3B, 8B, and 30B) share the same architectural design and follow the same training pipeline (base model, SFT, then multi-stage RL), each at its own scale. All three are strong reasoners and instruction followers. The clearest capability split shows up in post-training. The 8B and 30B models additionally go through an agentic RL block that teaches them to operate as agents: calling tools, editing and running code, driving a terminal, and searching the web inside real environments. Every model supports native tool calling. Served through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint (for example, with vLLM), it emits tool calls in the OpenAI function-calling format and plugs into agentic harnesses without extra glue. Granite 4.2 is also supported in SGLang, see the SGLang cookbook for a ready-to-serve recipe.

The rest of this post walks through the build: architecture, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, the multi-stage RL pipeline, and results.

Granite 4.2 models are built on a decoder-only dense transformer architecture with the following core components:.

Granite 4.2 models are post-trained from Granite-4.1 base models. Granite-4.1 base models were trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five-phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre-training, phases 3–4 perform mid-training with progressively higher-quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long-context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase uses a distinct data mixture and learning-rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web-scale data toward more curated, high-quality sources.

The pre-training recipe closely follows the previous generation; for a detailed treatment of the data blend, phase schedule, and long-context extension, see the Granite 4.1 blog.

Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) turns the base model into a reliable instruction-following, reasoning, and tool-using assistant. The SFT data mixture combines agentic (31.6%) and non-agentic (68.4%) data, totaling approximately 7.2 million samples, or roughly 100B tokens, of which about 65B are trainable.

The agentic corpus covers a broad range of domains, including software engineering (SWE, 69%), tool calling (12.1%), terminal use (8.0%), math (3.5%), search (0.8%), and action (0.2%). These samples and trajectories are generated using a diverse set of agent scaffolds and harnesses, including OpenHands, OpenCode, Terminus-2, SWE-agent, OpenResearcher, MiniSWE, OpenSeeker, EnvScaler, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Codex, and Goose. The agentic data combines samples from both open-source datasets and our own synthetically generated RL environments, spanning a variety of agent–harness combinations.

The non-agentic corpus consists of several major categories: instruction following (18.8%), coding (18.8%), math (14.6%), multilingual (7.0%), science (5.4%), reasoning (3.0%), and safety (0.8%).

Industry observers note that we apply multiple stages of quality control before a sample enters the final SFT mixture. First, data from different sources is normalized and reformatted into a consistent OpenAI Chat format, making the conversation structure and tool interactions uniform across datasets and scaffolds.

Industry observers note that we then use GPT-OSS-120B and Gemma 4 as LLM-based judges to assess sample quality. Low-scoring samples are removed, as are samples containing hallucinated or fabricated information, invalid tool interactions, or tool calls to functions that are not defined in the corresponding tool list. Several targeted, dataset-specific heuristic rules are also applied where appropriate to further improve quality and remove known sources of noise.

In a recent development, finally, we perform both local and global deduplication. Deduplication is based on SHA-256 hashes computed over the combination of the tools and messages fields, removing duplicate samples both within individual data sources and across the overall SFT mixture.

It has been revealed that the complete corpus is first globally shuffled to reduce ordering effects and ensure that samples from different domains are well mixed during training. The shuffled corpus is then partitioned into equally sized .parquet shards, which are tokenized using the model's tokenizer and chat template and prepared for large-scale distributed training.

Before launching the final large-scale runs, we tune hyperparameters on representative configurations, sweeping learning-rate schedules, initial learning rates, and warm-up ratios to find settings that train stably across model sizes. The final training configuration is summarized below:.

For the 30B model, we additionally perform a second phase of SFT focused specifically on agentic coding. In this phase, agentic, SWE, and coding data are upsampled to increase their effective contribution to the training distribution, while approximately 16% of the mixture is retained as replay data from the original SFT corpus.

Sources indicate that the 30B model is then fine-tuned for roughly one additional epoch at a lower learning rate of 3.0e-6. This targeted second phase increases the model's exposure to agentic coding trajectories without discarding the capabilities acquired during the initial SFT phase.

In a recent development, after SFT, we apply a multi-stage, multi-environment reinforcement learning pipeline. Rather than a single RL pass, we run a chain of focused stages spanning many environments: math, code, science, instruction following, tool use, and structured output, then software engineering, terminal use, and web search. Each stage is an independent RL run that targets one capability and warm-starts from the previous stage's checkpoint.

Figure 1. The staged RL curriculum. Foundational RL (verifiable rewards + skill boosters) runs for all sizes; the agentic RL block (SWE → Terminal → Search) runs for 8B and 30B only. Every model finishes with RLHF. Each stage is a separate GRPO run that warm-starts from the previous checkpoint.

Every stage trains with asynchronous GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), so the generator and trainer halves of the loop never block on each other. A pool of generation workers keeps sampling responses and dropping the finished trajectories into a shared buffer; once the buffer holds a full step's worth, the trainer pulls that batch, takes an optimizer step, and streams the updated parameters back to the generator workers without pausing them. A refresh can land partway through a rollout, leaving a single trajectory stitched together from two adjacent policy versions. We allow this instead of paying to prevent it: the workers reuse their existing KV cache rather than rebuilding it after each refresh, and the one guardrail is a limit that keeps them from drifting more than a single revision behind the trainer, which bounds how off-policy any sample can get. Whatever mismatch survives that limit is handled in the objective by truncated importance sampling, which clamps the train-versus-generation log-probability ratio to a fixed ceiling so a handful of stale tokens cannot dominate an update.

Advantages are group-relative with a leave-one-out baseline: each response is judged against the mean reward of the other samples drawn for the same prompt, which removes the need for a separate value network. To make this concrete, take RLVR, the first and longest-running stage: each step pairs 256 prompts with 16 sampled responses apiece for a 4,096-example batch, which the trainer consumes in a single optimizer step before the next rollout begins. Later stages keep this machinery unchanged and adjust only the per-stage shape, shown next.

It has been revealed that the pipeline keeps a common backbone of hyperparameters across every stage, which makes the curriculum easier to run and compare. A handful of knobs are fixed everywhere:.

What changes from stage to stage is the shape of each run: how many prompts and generations per step, how long the context is, whether the agent loop runs, and how hard we pull back toward the reference policy. The table below gives the exact settings for the 30B chain, stage by stage:.

According to recent reports, parameters shown for the 30B model. Global batch size = prompts/step × generations/prompt (e.g. 256 × 16 = 4096 for RLVR). The 3B and 8B models use the same recipe and hyperparameters with fewer stages (see How the Three Sizes Differ); the stage list is what changes, not the knobs.

It has been revealed that the KL schedule follows the reward type: explore freely where the reward is objective and verifiable (RLVR and SWE 2 run at KL 0), and stay close to the reference where the objective is preference, safety, or a narrow skill graft (RLHF and the code booster use KL 0.05). The rollout-turns column counts the environment interactions GRPO itself sees per rollout. In every case the model is trained on complete, real-environment trajectories.

Each stage is a separate RL run with a single objective and its own reward signal. When it finishes, its policy is exported to Hugging Face format and becomes the base model for the next stage, so the pipeline is a sequence of warm-starts:.

The 8B and 30B models follow the full ladder. The 3B model takes a shortened path: foundational RL and alignment, without the agentic block.

A stage is defined mostly by how it is rewarded. Across the pipeline there are three reward types, and a single stage can use more than one:.

Verifiable rewards are objective and hard to game, so the pipeline front-loads them. Judge- and preference-based rewards handle open-ended qualities that no checker can express. Agentic-outcome rewards are the sparsest: often a single bit at the end of a long tool-use trajectory.

RLVR is the foundational stage and the broadest data mix in the pipeline: a single blended dataset spanning many verifiable domains.

According to recent reports, each task type carries its own verifier, so the reward is grounded per example. RLVR runs for two rounds on 3B and 8B, and three on 30B. Each round is a fresh warm-started run on a re-weighted mix of public and internally curated RL data.

After RLVR, a few short booster stages sharpen specific capabilities that benefit from concentrated training focusing on the following domains:.

Boosters are small, focused runs. A light KL penalty keeps the model close to its current behavior while nudging one skill.

In the agentic stages the model learns to act: call tools, observe results, and iterate inside a real environment, rewarded on whether the task was actually solved. These stages share the same shape: multi-turn tool use, real (not simulated) environments, sparse outcome rewards, and GRPO, warm-started from the coding-boosted checkpoint. They run in order: SWE → Terminal → Search.

It has been revealed that figure 2. The three agentic-RL environments. Each pairs a real harness with a real environment and a sparse, outcome-based reward. The 3B model runs none of these.

The final stage of every model is RLHF for human preference and safety. It optimizes against a generative reward model (GenRM) for preference, plus a safety reward covering jailbreak resistance and appropriate refusals. This stage uses the highest KL penalty in the pipeline, aligning tone and safety without eroding the capabilities the earlier stages built. In addition to human preference and safety alignment, this stage also applies a reasoning-length penalty to discourage overly verbose reasoning behavior acquired during earlier stages.

Same method and infrastructure; the difference is how far up the ladder each model goes.

3B is a strong foundational-RL model; 8B and 30B add the agentic-RL block on top, learning to act with tools in real environments.

Reinforcement learning at this scale needs infrastructure that can drive a training loop and a fleet of live environments at the same time. This matters most in the agentic stages, where every training example is a multi-turn rollout that edits code, runs commands, or browses the web. Granite 4.2's RL runs on two open components: NeMo-RL on the training side and NeMo-Gym on the rollout side.

Sources indicate that figure 3. The RL system. NeMo-RL drives the GRPO loop (Megatron-Core training backend, vLLM generation, and Megatron-Bridge for HF⇄Megatron weight conversion). NeMo-Gym orchestrates rollouts and hosts the tools, sandboxes, and reward/verifier calls as pluggable Resources.

That uniformity is what makes the staged curriculum above practical: a booster's rule-based checker and a full SWE sandbox present the same interface to GRPO.

This split is also what makes the asynchronous training loop described above physically possible: generation and policy updates live on separate GPU pools, so the expensive generation fleet — including the live agentic environments — stays busy instead of idling through optimizer steps.

According to recent reports, granite 4.2 was evaluated across agentic coding, general agentic and tool use, reasoning, chat and instruction following, and long context. The full benchmark table is below, followed by charts that break out the headline results by model size.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

The charts below break these results out by capability area.

Recent findings suggest that figure 4. Reasoning (pass@1). Scores rise consistently with model size across math (AIME25, HMMT), science (GPQA), and code reasoning (LiveCodeBench, SciCode).

Figure 5. Agentic coding resolve rates. The agentic-RL block is trained only for 8B and 30B; the 30B model leads across SWE-Bench variants and Terminal-Bench.

According to recent reports, figure 6. General agentic and tool-use benchmarks, reported for all three sizes.

Recent findings suggest that we also released four quantized variants of the Granite 4.2 models for inference with vLLM. The models are converted to FP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using LLM Compressor, and to the GGUF format using the llama.cpp framework for reduced-memory deployment.

In a recent development, the FP8 version is quantized with dynamic per-channel weights and per-token activations. No calibration is used.

The NVFP4 and MXFP4 versions are quantized using GPTQ calibrated on 2K samples drawn from the SFT dataset. Max context length is 2K during calibration.

Conversion of the Granite 4.2 models to GGUF is done with the canonical llama.cpp tool as described in https://github.com/IBM/gguf#gguf-conversion--quantization.

Several GGUF formats are provided:.

We trained the Granite 4.2 language models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted by CoreWeave, featuring:.

This infrastructure delivers the high-bandwidth, low-latency communication required for efficient large-scale distributed training.

Sources indicate that the training software stack is packaged into .sqsh container images, each giving a run a reproducible, portable environment with its SBSA-compatible CUDA targets, Linux aarch64 Python wheels, and GPU-specific binaries pinned. The large-scale SFT runs build on an NGC PyTorch base image (Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.8, Python 3.12); the RL stack runs in its own NeMo-RL container.

Granite models support tool calling with integrated reasoning: the model reasons about which tool to call and why before calling it. Tools are defined with the OpenAI function definition schema.

Granite models can serve as the backbone for agentic coding tools. Because they support reasoning and tool calling through the OpenAI-compatible API, they integrate with popular agentic harnesses without extra adapters. Start the vLLM server, then follow the harness-specific instructions below.

Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json:.

Configure ~/.pi/agent/models.json:.

Then select the granite-4.2-30b model with /model or Ctrl+L in the interactive session.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until latest hire lands, then stick around as advisor.
  • Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the manufacturer’s board can find his successor.
  • Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register noted he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rajiv Ramaswami will stay in the chair until latest hire lands, then stick around as advisor.

Nutanix CEO Rajiv Ramaswami has decided to step down from the job once the manufacturer’s board can find his successor.

Ramaswami announced his decision on Tuesday and in conversation with The Register noted he doesn’t have another job lined up, isn’t sure what he will do next, fancies sitting on boards or advising startups, but will take a break after Nutanix finds its next leader.

The CEO moved from VMware to Nutanix in 2020 and characterized his time at the company as writing its “second chapter.” The first, he explained, saw Nutanix focus on hyperconverged infrastructure (HCI) and a limited group of workloads, especially desktop virtualization, while struggling to make a profit.

According to recent reports, in chapter two, Nutanix redefined HCI as “hybrid cloud infrastructure” by enabling its stack to run on-prem or in public clouds, and by adding support for containers alongside VMs. Ramaswami took credit for stabilizing Nutanix’s finances while leading the expansion of its platform and for keeping net promoter scores high while the company grew.

According to recent reports, the CEO added that Nutanix’s decision to end its devotion to virtualized storage and start to support external arrays was also part of chapter two. Ramaswami noted he hopes to expand the number of storage vendors Nutanix supports beyond Dell, Everpure, and NetApp, until it works with all major array suppliers.

Chapter 3, he said, will be making Nutanix an AI platform, “by catering to a whole upcoming set of ecosystems.”.

Industry observers note that ramaswami told The Register he had been thinking about moving on for some time and raised it with the board in recent weeks. In the letter he wrote to Nutanix staff, the CEO remarked the manufacturer's board has begun the search for a successor and said he will remain at his post until a replacement is found and then “continue to serve as a senior advisor to the company for a period of time.”.

It has been revealed that news of the CEO’s planned departure came on the same day Nutanix revealed its Q1 results, which saw 15 percent revenue growth to $772.4 million. The company added 410 customers in the quarter, the slowest growth for several years. Ramaswami stated high hardware costs remain “a headwind” for Nutanix, but said the company continues to win customers seeking an alternative to VMware. He also pointed to the largest fresh customer win for the quarter coming from a financial services outfit that uses Dell external storage, a significant score because two years ago Nutanix could not have competed for that business.

Nutanix forecast slightly faster growth for the rest of its financial year, suggesting it is not ready to ride AI’s rocket to riches. Investors knocked about ten percent off the company’s share price in after-hours trading, sending it to around $50, roughly double what it was when Ramaswami took over as CEO, but below $79-plus peaks in late 2025. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo.
  • In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition.
  • It has been revealed that AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also upcoming ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

It has been revealed that AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

Recent findings suggest that headlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough highlights a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Sources indicate that amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

In a recent development, amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Industry observers note that amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – Latest Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Latest with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

It has been revealed that optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

In a recent development, AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

It has been revealed that AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Sources indicate that join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!
