#207144. Latest Update: Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 Reaches the Top

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4323 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Chipsandcheese ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 Reaches the Top

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4323 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Chipsandcheese

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings.
  • The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively.
  • Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that qualcomm’s laptop effort had humble beginnings. Their early Arm-based laptops used cell phone SoCs, and suffered from noticeably poor performance even against lower end Intel chips. But breaking into the PC market was going to be a marathon rather than a sprint, and Qualcomm has been persistent. Qualcomm created higher performance Snapdragon variants targeted at laptops, which became increasingly competent with each generation. Now, Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme can deliver CPU performance that challenges the best of its x86-64 competition. To deliver that performance, Qualcomm relies on the third generation of their in-house Oryon architecture, which I’ll call Oryon 3 for short.

The Snapdragon X2 Elite deploys Oryon 3 in both E-Core and P-Core variants, which Qualcomm confusingly calls “performance” and “prime” cores, respectively. P-Cores are the star of the show in the Snapdragon X2 Elite, where they provide both maximum single threaded performance while also providing the bulk of multithreaded throughput. That’s because Qualcomm has P-Cores outnumber their E-Cores by a factor of two, creating an inverted hybrid strategy compared to Intel’s. Thanks to this strategy, Qualcomm’s Oryon 3 P-Core variant shoulders most of the burden when it comes to Qualcomm’s PC market ambitions.

Oryon 3 takes on this burden by deploying an architecture with a strong resemblance to the first Oryon generation. Qualcomm technically has a second generation Oryon core, but only used it in phones. Their website also suggests it’s a very minor change over the first generation, so I’ll be treating first generation Oryon as Oryon 3’s direct predecessor.

Similarity to Oryon 1 is a good thing, because that gives Oryon 3 just about everything you could ask for from a 2026-era high performance design. From Oryon 1, Oryon 3 inherits an out-of-order window in excess of 600 micro-ops. Qualcomm has also carried forward a two-level cache setup that emphasizes speed over capacity. Compared to its predecessor, Oryon 3 takes things up a notch by pushing clock speeds to 5 GHz. It’s a huge 16% increase over the 4.3 GHz speed that Oryon 1 could reach, and is enough to offer a generational performance gain on its own. But Qualcomm doesn’t stop there. Oryon 3 increases core width to 9 micro-ops, up from 8 in its predecessor, and makes a number of improvements throughout the pipeline. Qualcomm brings SVE2 and SME support to the newly introduced core as well, keeping it up-to-date with the evolving aarch64 architecture and opening up new software optimization opportunities. In its role as a maximum performance architecture, Oryon 3 faces off against the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove. Arm’s Cortex X925 is another competitor, thanks to Nvidia’s laptop push with N1X.

Setting aside clock speed, Oryon 3’s headline architectural improvement is a core width increase from 8 to 9 ups. At the frontend, Qualcomm supports this by adding another decode slot. The fetch and decode pipeline otherwise looks mostly unchanged. Oryon 1 already had over-provisioned instruction cache bandwidth at 64 bytes per cycle, which is more than sufficient to feed a 8-wide or 9-wide aarch64 decoder. Qualcomm has also kept a 192 KB, 6-way instruction cache with hardware coherency, as well as a 256 entry 8-way instruction TLB. These large structures should help the core use its fastest instruction delivery path more often than its peers, which have smaller instruction caches and instruction TLBs. Impressively, Qualcomm managed to keep these large structures and add an extra decode slot while keeping a 13 cycle branch mispredict penalty. Clock speed increases often come with compromises like longer pipelines or smaller structures, but here Qualcomm is able to have their cake and eat it too.

Testing instruction bandwidth with a stream of NOPs validates the increased decoder width when the test loop fits within the instruction cache. Improvements continue at larger instruction footprints. Oryon 3 is able to sustain about 4 NOPs/cycle from L2, compared to 2 per cycle on Oryon 1. Qualcomm might have changed something with instruction prefetching from L2, or they might have widened datapaths between the instruction cache and L2. Whatever the case, Oryon 3 now matches the likes of AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Coves in terms of streaming code from L2, while boasting a much larger L2. AMD and Intel’s cores do have a L3 that provides more capacity than Qualcomm’s L2, but fetching code from that L3 will cause another drop in instruction throughput.

Industry observers note that high core throughput places pressure on the branch predictor, which must follow the instruction stream fast enough to keep the core fed. Oryon 3 improves by expanding its predecessor’s ability to handle taken branches back-to-back. Oryon 1 could only do “zero-bubble” taken branches within a 8 KB instruction footprint. Oryon 3 can do so within a 2048 branch footprint, regardless of branch spacing and code footprint. Perhaps Qualcomm switched to using a fully decoupled 2048 entry BTB. Realistically, that means Oryon 3 should be able to do zero-bubble taken branches over a branch footprint 2x to 4x larger than its predecessor, considering typical branch spacing.

Compared to AMD and Intel’s latest cores, Qualcomm lacks any ability to handle more than one taken branch per cycle. Arm’s newer cores are also capable of doing two taken branches per cycle. I suspect AMD, Arm, and Intel decided that handling multiple taken branches per cycle became more profitable once their cores got wide enough, so seeing Qualcomm build a very wide core without that ability is surprising. Perhaps clock speed factors into that decision, because going from 4.3 to 5 GHz is a huge jump. If so, Qualcomm’s choice would be justified because a clock speed increase of that magnitude probably offers a larger performance increase than going for two taken branches per cycle. Of course, it’s impossible to know if branch predictor paths presented a timing challenge for Oryon.

For branches with dynamic taken/not-taken behavior, Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle conditional predictor. Testing with branches whose outcomes correlate with increasingly long history lengths shows an average 0.5 cycle increase in time per branch over an always- taken reference run, as long as the test stays within the conditional predictor’s capabilities. Because I randomly generate patterns so that each branch is taken roughly 50% of the time, a 0.5 cycle average penalty suggests Qualcomm only incurs the 2-cycle timing if the direction predictor disagrees with a base prediction. Direction prediction starts falling apart with more than 32K patterns in play, which is an improvement over the approximately 24K patterns that first generation Oryon could handle in this test.

For comparison, Zen 5’s conditional predictor can handle roughly 48K patterns before falling apart. Unlike Oryon 3, and unlike some older Zen generations, Zen 5 does not show an increase in branch latency compared to an always-taken pattern.

Recent findings suggest that indirect branches can go to multiple targets, and present another level of difficulty because the branch predictor has to select between previously seen targets, and must store more than one target per branch. Oryon 3 has a 2-cycle indirect predictor that can track 2048 indirect targets, matching its predecessor.

Industry observers note that A single branch can jump to 256 targets without incurring a significant penalty. This could mean at least eight of the bits that Oryon 3 uses to index into its indirect target array are influenced by branch history.

A 50 entry return stack handles return predictions, just as on Oryon 1. However, testing reveals that Oryon 3 can use all 50 entries before hitting a performance degradation. When call depth exceeds return stack capacity, Oryon 3 degrades gracefully rather than immediately taking a drastic penalty as Oryon 1 does. Oryon 1’s performance drop is heavy enough to suggest it’s mispredicting every return after the return stack overflows.

It has been revealed that perhaps Qualcomm implemented a new mechanism to keep a single overflow from messing up the entire return stack, and lets Oryon 3 only mispredict returns whose addresses get forced out on an overflow. Whatever this optimization is, it gives Oryon 3 return prediction behavior in-line with many other cores, including AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Skymont. In capacity terms, AMD’s Zen 5 has a slightly larger 52 entry return stack.

Optimizations at the rename and allocate stage on Qualcomm’s major core are remarkably similar to those on its little core counterpart. Both cores can eliminate up to two register-to-register MOVs per cycle. They can also eliminate up to two add-immediate instructions, as long as their immediates sum to 255 or less. It’s slightly strange that Qualcomm has kept the same optimization capability even though the big core is more than twice as wide as its little core companion. That results in degraded microbenchmark figures when I chain dependent MOVs or add-immediate instructions without a break, because the wider core can get more of those instructions into the same rename group, which means the two-per-cycle restriction causes more missed optimization opportunities.

It has been revealed that one of the best strategies in CPU architecture is to avoid changing something that isn’t broken. Oryon 3’s backend at a high level is basically identical to the one in its predecessor. That makes sense because if Oryon 1 encountered performance challenges, they likely had little to do with its backend strategy. Qualcomm specifies a reorder buffer capacity of over 650 micro-ops for both Oryon 1 and Oryon 3. Microbenchmarking puts capacity at 675 micro-ops for Oryon 3, and 680 on Oryon 1. Register files and memory ordering queues see little to no movement in size as well.

It has been revealed that qualcomm’s choice to avoid major backend changes is justified, because Oryon 3’s backend structures remain competitively sized even against emerging competition like AMD’s Zen 6. Execution throughput also remains competitive. Oryon 3 does have slightly smaller memory ordering queues, and weaker vector execution throughput compared to its x86-64 counterparts. The latter comes down to having a smaller 128-bit vector width, which is especially a disadvantage against Zen 5. However, that should only affect a small minority of applications.

Recent findings suggest that even though Oryon 3’s backend is similar to its predecessor, there’s still plenty of change under the hood. Predication is a central feature in SVE2 and SME, so Oryon 3 gets a new 120 entry predicate register file. The predicate registers themselves only have to be 16 bits wide because of Oryon 3’s 128-bit vector length. But while the predicate register file doesn’t need a lot of storage, it does need to be hooked up to every major execution unit block. Predicate generation can happen from both the scalar and vector side. All four vector pipes and four load/store pipes support predication, meaning a lot of reads from the predicate register file.

Sources indicate that new SVE2 and SME instructions also require changes to backend logic. SVE’s vector length agnostic design rides heavily on predicate generation instructions like those of the WHILE* variety (like WHILELO). Oryon 3 breaks WHILE* instructions into two micro-ops, which execute through the integer pipes to deliver a throughput of one WHILE* instruction per cycle. Predicate generation instructions that don’t require a GPR input, like PTRUE and CMPEQ, execute through two FP/vector pipes. Besides predication focused changes, SVE2 adds new math instructions like CDOT, meaning more execution unit functionality behind the vector/FP ports.

Industry observers note that like Oryon 1, Oryon 3 has a four-pipe load/store unit. Memory dependencies are handled by a robust store forwarding mechanism, which can do fast forwarding for all cases where a load overlaps a prior store. Oryon 3 is able to do that even when the load isn’t contained within the older store, meaning the load/store unit is able to combine data from both an in-flight store and data fetched from the L1 data cache. A dependent store+load pair has a latency of 6 cycles on the integer side, or 8 cycles on the vector/FP side. While Oryon 3 can’t do zero-latency store forwarding the way AMD’s Zen 5 and Intel’s Lion Cove can, the ability to avoid the 14 or 19 cycle penalty those cores take in partial overlap cases is quite nice. Arm’s Cortex X925 has the weakest store forwarding capabilities of the bunch, with no zero-cycle capability and a 12-13 cycle partial overlap penalty.

In a recent development, for independent accesses, Oryon 3 prefers 16B alignment for stores. Stores that cross a 16B boundary take a slight penalty, though curiously there’s no penalty for crossing a 64B cacheline boundary. Perhaps Oryon 3 has a special optimization for speeding up line-crossing stores. The same characteristics apply on the vector side.

According to recent reports, SVE introduces scatter and gather functionality to the load/store unit, forcing it to handle possibly non-contiguous accesses from a single instruction. Testing with LD1W gathers (32-bit elements) achieves a core-wide throughput of 1-2 elements per cycle. Gathers therefore have lower throughput not just compared to contiguous loads, but also equivalent scalar loads. However, Oryon 3 has an optimization that allows repeated gather loads to the same address to execute at 4/cycle. Gathers therefore seem capable of using all four LSU pipes, and don’t go down a smaller subset of specialized pipes. However, the general case seems to rely on a complex flow that involves several micro-ops, resulting in lower throughput.

Recent findings suggest that dependent gathers have 14 cycle latency, which is acceptable for a non-contiguous load operation. Zen 5 handles vaguely equivalent AVX2 gathers with 19 cycle latency.

The load/store unit also has to translate program-visible virtual addresses to physical addresses that correspond to DRAM locations (or possibly MMIO). Qualcomm sized up the L1 DTLB from a 224 entry 7-way structure on Oryon 1, to a 256 entry 8-way one on Oryon 3. Perhaps Qualcomm always intended for the L1 DTLB to be 256 entries and 8-way set associative like the instruction-side L1 TLB, but couldn’t fit the last way into Oryon 1. A 256 entry L1 DTLB covers 1 MB of address space using 4 KB pages, which is a lot compared to the smaller L1 DTLBs on other designs. An 8K entry L2 TLB handles larger memory footprints, and serves both instruction and data accesses. The L2 TLB’s capacity is also impressive compared to the competition.

It has been revealed that comparing with Zen 5 can be complicated because AMD can opportunistically use a single TLB entry to cover up to four consecutive 4 KB pages, provided the translations have the same attributes and lead to contiguous physical pages. Zen 5 can cover more address space with its TLBs despite a lower entry count if it can make maximum use of that page coalescing capability, though I don’t have data on how effective that is in practice.

Testing with performance counters validates Qualcomm’s large TLB sizes. The core’s PMU indicates a rise in L1D TLB misses after 1 MB, when testing accesses with a 4 KB stride. L2 TLB misses rise after 32 MB, though they only sharply increase after 64 MB.

Qualcomm specifies 2-cycle latency for L2 TLB accesses, which would be incredible for a 8K entry L2 TLB. However, comparing L2 latency with 4 KB and 2 MB pages suggests that a L2 TLB hit costs at least an extra 6-7 cycles of latency.

In a recent development, qualcomm’s Snapdragon X Elite used a two-level caching strategy that emphasizes speed over the ability to scale last level cache capacity and the number of cores served by each last level cache instance. For the Snapdragon X2 Elite Qualcomm upgraded the cache subsystem by increasing L2 capacity from 12 to 16 MB for the P-Core clusters. This cache capacity increase boosts the amount of cache a single core can allocate into. It also helps account for each cluster having six cores instead of four, though cache per core still drops slightly from 3 MB on Oryon 1 to 2.66 MB in Oryon 3.

According to recent reports, 16 MB of CPU-side last level cache isn’t large by 2026 standards. AMD’s standard Zen 5 configurations use 32 MB of L3 cache, while Intel’s Arrow Lake has 36 MB of L3. However, Qualcomm’s caching capacity is fine next to the 16 MB of L3 that AMD puts in their mainstream Strix Point mobile chip’s performance cluster, and Qualcomm makes their L2 fast for the capacity it provides. With 20-23 cycle latency depending on which core is making the access, Qualcomm’s L2 can return data faster than the 46 cycle latency that AMD’s optimization guide specifies for Zen 5’s L3. AMD’s 46 cycle figure seems to apply to configurations with 32 MB of L3, like on the Ryzen 9 9900X. A Zen 5 variant with 96 MB of L3 incurs several extra cycles of latency, showing how a triple level cache subsystem can enable last level cache capacity scaling because the core-private L2 cache reduces sensitivity to L3 latency. Intel’s Lion Cove is Oryon 3’s opposite with respect to caching strategy, with four cache levels to enable capacity/speed tradeoffs at L2 and L3.

20+ cycles of L2 latency is still high compared to 14 cycles on AMD’s Zen 5, so Oryon 3 uses a large 96 KB 6-way L1D. Unusually for a high frequency design, Oryon 3 achieves 3 cycle L1D latency. It’s an impressive achievement, because even Arm’s lower clocked Cortex X925 has 4 cycle latency to a smaller 64 KB L1D.

Oryon 3 only reveals a slight latency increase as a pointer chasing test spills out of the L1D when using a 64 byte stride. Using a shorter stride increases the length of the pointer chasing chain, and more clearly shows the L1D’s capacity. Qualcomm seems to have a “correlated miss caching” (CMC) style prefetcher like many of Arm’s designs, which tracks when a cache miss for one address is likely to be followed by a second miss to another address. This type of prefetcher can follow pointer chasing chains and defeat latency testing if the tested chain falls within what the prefetcher can remember. If Qualcomm is doing this, and they do suggest it by indicating they have “pointer” prefetching algorithms, then the data above points to it being a L1D prefetcher.

Arm in contrast places their CMC prefetcher at L2, which lets it be more aggressive because a larger L2 cache is less sensitive to having some capacity wasted by useless prefetches. For example, the CMC prefetcher on Arm’s Cortex A78 is able to reduce latency across the Mediatek Genio 1200’s 2 MB L3 when testing with a 64B stride compared to a 8B stride (at least 32K pointer destination predictions compared to 8K on Oryon 3).

According to recent reports, oryon 3’s L1D can service four accesses per cycle, all four of which can be loads, and two of which can be stores. Compared to Zen 5 and Lion Cove, Oryon 3’s maximum load bandwidth is held back by its 128-bit vector width. However, Oryon 3 should remain very competitive when running code that can’t be well vectorized, or vectorized code that doesn’t scale to longer vector lengths.

In a recent development, L2 bandwidth is just under 32B/cycle for reads, in terms of how much data the core can get into registers. Qualcomm states that each core has a 64B/cycle datapath to L2. This can be validated by only accessing the first 128 bits of each 64B line, and treating that as loading the entire line because cache fills happen at 64B line granularity. Doing so gives about 48B/cycle of inferred L2 to L1D bandwidth. A read-modify-write pattern that creates equal traffic in both the L1D fill and writeback directions also reaches 48B/cycle.

Sources indicate that I have a separate piece for more on the Snapdragon X2 Elite’s system level memory subsystem characteristics. Overall though, there’s a lot to like about Oryon 3’s memory subsystem. As long as you don’t benefit from having more than 16 MB of last level cache in each core cluster, Qualcomm’s cache setup should be more than a match for the triple level setups used by Intel, AMD, and other Arm cores.

Because running Linux on the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme is complicated at the moment and difficult considering other time constraints (Chips and Cheese isn’t a job after all, and I have a real job to pay attention to), I tested SPEC CPU2026 using Windows Subsystem on Linux. I’m pinning the vmmemWSL process to a P-Core for predictability. Results show the Oryon 3 P-Core delivering desktop-level SPEC CPU2026 integer scores, even though it’s implemented in a laptop. That’s an impressive showing because desktop chips enjoy advantages like higher cache capacity, lower DRAM latency, and higher clock speeds. A comparison against a typical AMD or Intel mobile part would almost certainly hand Oryon 3 a victory rather than a tie.

Qualcomm does score slightly behind Zen 5 in SPEC’s floating point suite, but manages to stay ahead of Intel. Individual subtests show modest differences between the cores, though there are outliers. 706.stockfish for example hands Zen 5 a large win, because GCC 14.2.0 was able to vectorize a large part of it to use AVX-512.

However, AVX-512 does not give AMD a huge lead in SPEC’s floating point workloads. 749.fotonik3d and 765.roms execute a lot of AVX-512 instructions on Zen 5, but Oryon 3 is able to compensate with higher IPC. Both workloads tend to be more memory bound as well, reducing the benefit of AMD’s higher vector throughput.

Further performance analysis is difficult without more work because WSL only passes through a subset of performance monitoring events. However, there’s enough data to show that Qualcomm’s branch prediction accuracy is up there with the best. Overall branch prediction accuracy is actually a bit better than that of AMD’s Zen 5. Oryon 3 even scores a win in 723.llvm, which is SPEC CPU2026’s toughest branch prediction workload.

Performance counters also show the merit of Oryon 3’s large L1D. L1D cache sizes have remained stubbornly stagnant outside of Qualcomm (and Apple) cores. In 1998, AMD rolled out their Athlon core with a 64 KB L1 data cache. No current cores from AMD, Intel, or Arm have a larger L1D, and I don’t put Lion Cove’s 192 KB “level 1 of the level 1 cache” in the same category as a conventional L1D because of its higher latency.

Each vendor’s performance monitoring unit accounts for L1D misses differently, but the differences are large enough to show that Qualcomm can service a lot more requests out of its fastest cache level than Intel or AMD.

According to recent reports, third generation Oryon is a top-notch core with everything needed to succeed on a level playing field. Qualcomm has given their core a large out-of-order engine, is able to run it at 5 GHz, and feeds it with a competent branch predictor and a low latency cache setup. Oryon 3 joins Arm’s Cortex X925 in delivering desktop-level performance, and both Arm cores should be seen as serious pacing challenges for Intel and AMD.

Sources indicate that oryon 3 isn’t perfect of course. A wider SVE vector width could improve its situation relative to Zen 5 in vectorized workloads. Going to six vector/floating point pipes like in Arm’s Cortex X925 is an option too, though it may be difficult to pull off without regressing clock speeds. Qualcomm’s branch predictor could pick up some of the two taken branches per cycle goodness that’s now common on AMD, Arm, and Intel cores. Cache capacity could be an problem too, because a two-level cache setup forces a tightly coupled L2 design to meet latency requirements. That could make cache capacity difficult to scale.

It has been revealed that all of those are areas for improvement, rather than significant weaknesses. SPEC scores for example show that a core doesn’t need to sustain two taken branches per cycle to be up there with the best, at least not in this generation. As for cache capacity, I can’t think of a consumer scenario where that makes a huge impact except for gaming. Games of course struggle with a binary translation issue, which is outside Qualcomm’s control.

Binary translation does bring up a problem for Oryon 3 though, because having a good core is only one piece of the puzzle. The software ecosystem that Qualcomm has to work with is a persistent sticking point, because while Windows on Arm has improved over the years, it’s still not as polished as a native x86-64 setup. Qualcomm has also struggled with Linux support. It’s a missed opportunity, because Linux is increasingly being seen as a strong alternative to Windows due to Windows 11’s misplaced priorities. Linux applications are also more likely to have aarch64 versions, minimising the importance of binary translation. Beyond the software ecosystem, Qualcomm’s laptop push faces headwinds because high DRAM costs push consumers to defer buying upcoming devices. Laptops with soldered memory are especially vulnerable, because there’s no chance of buying a device with less memory with hopes of upgrading it later once prices drop. These challenges must be frustrating for hardware engineers who worked on Oryon 3, because they’ve built their most competitive CPU architecture yet, but need more puzzle pieces to fall into place.

Recent findings suggest that I hope Qualcomm continues to run the marathon of breaking into the PC market, and the puzzle pieces line up soon to enable success. Oryon 3 is an excellent core. I’ve used the Zenbook A16 laptop sampled by Asus on a recent casual trip, and used it as a daily driver for a few weeks. The laptop is subjectively as fast as my desktop back at home, and highlights just how far Qualcomm has gone. I want to see the people who worked on it rewarded for what they achieved. I also hope to see the Oryon line grow with future generations, and keep pushing the leading edge of single threaded performance.

Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning with Tunix and Gemma 4 on Google TPUs

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we demonstrated how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs.
  • We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host.

In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we demonstrated how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 26 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3714 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more.
  • Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class.
  • Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my finetuned multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical model, trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 alongside this blogpost, easily outperforms every general-purpose retrieval model I could find on my medical retrieval evaluation: dense, sparse, lexical, and multi-vector alike.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more. Its v6.0 update introduces a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, alongside a complete training approach for it. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a multi-vector model that outperforms general-purpose retrievers on your data. This method can also train strong newly introduced multi-vector models from scratch. Everything below runs on pip install -U "sentence-transformers[train]".

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my finetuned multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical model, trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 alongside this blogpost, easily outperforms every general-purpose retrieval model I could find on my medical retrieval evaluation: dense, sparse, lexical, and multi-vector alike.

If you're interested in finetuning dense embedding models, sparse embedding models, or rerankers instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models, Training and Finetuning Sparse Embedding Models, and Training and Finetuning Reranker Models blogposts.

This blogpost is about training multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to use them, from loading and encoding to indexing in vector databases, see the companion Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

Recent findings suggest that A dense embedding model compresses a whole text into a single vector, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model) skips that compression. It keeps one small vector per token and scores a query against a document with the MaxSim operator, where every query token finds its best-matching document token and the scores are summed. Token-level matching preserves exactly the fine-grained signals that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval, at the cost of a bigger index.

The companion Multi-Vector Embedding Models blogpost covers the architecture, encoding, scoring, and indexing in detail, so I'll keep this section short and get to the training.

According to recent reports, finetuning multi-vector models significantly improves their retrieval performance on your specific domain: the vocabulary, the query style, and the notion of relevance all differ between web search, legal discovery, code search, and scientific literature review. Because queries and documents are matched token by token, multi-vector models pick up fine-grained domain signals that single-vector models tend to average away, and they respond very well to even modest amounts of in-domain finetuning data.

Beyond that, most released retrieval models were configured for short passages. The classic ColBERT checkpoints truncate documents at 180 or 300 tokens, and many popular dense models at 256 or 512, because their MS MARCO-style training data rarely goes beyond that. If your documents are long, these models silently discard most of every document before scoring it. On my medical evaluation with passages averaging 941 tokens, I measured that this truncation costs up to 0.24 NDCG@10, considerably more than any difference between model architectures. When you train your own model, you configure the document length that your data needs.

LightOn ran into this same dynamic with code retrieval, where general LateOn wasn't enough and they trained LateOn-Code. Your domain, whether that's medical, legal, financial, or your manufacturer's internal documents, is not getting an official model. This blogpost reveals you how to build it yourself, in a matter of hours, on a single consumer GPU.

Training MultiVectorEncoder models involves the following components:.

Let's take a closer look at each component.

Multi-vector training gives you a real choice of starting point, and it matters more than you might expect.

If you want to further finetune an existing multi-vector model, you don't have to worry about the architecture at all:.

The checkpoint brings its own recipe along: its query and document marker tokens, its projection head, its scoring skiplist. For finetuning, you generally want to keep all of that and change only what your data demands. The first thing to check is the length configuration, since many released checkpoints cap documents at 180 to 512 tokens (see Why Finetune?), and my medical passages run to 1,400 tokens. The mLateOn family already serves the backbone's full 8192 token context, but if your starting checkpoint carries caps, lift them:.

With the per-task caps unset, truncation falls back to the tokenizer's model_max_length, which is why I configure that limit at load time above.

I made one more change, adding a punctuation skiplist that excludes punctuation tokens from document-side scoring and storage. In a 4-way ablation (none, punctuation, stopwords, both) it modestly won on quality, and it shrinks the document index by 9.6% on this data for free:.

You can also point MultiVectorEncoder at any base transformer, and a fresh, randomly initialized token-level projection is appended for you:.

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them down to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. The projection starts random, so training is required before this model is useful. Interestingly, this works with strong dense embedding backbones too. A fresh projection on Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base reached within 0.03 of the existing-checkpoint starting points in my experiments, from nothing but the projection and 25k training pairs.

The classic ColBERT tokenization tricks ([MASK] query expansion, [Q] / [D] prefix tokens, a document length cap, a punctuation skiplist) are all off by default and configurable. See Creating Custom Models for the full set. For what it's worth, I tested [MASK] query expansion in four configurations for my domain finetune and none of them made a measurable difference, so don't feel obliged to reach for the classic recipe.

I measured this directly while preparing this blogpost, taking six starting points and training each with the identical recipe on 25k medical question-passage pairs from MIRIAD, then evaluating on 1,000 held-out questions against a 50,000 passage corpus:.

The result surprised me, and it replicated across two model families. *The -unsupervised checkpoints adapt to a fresh domain far better than their finished siblings, overtaking them despite starting lower. These checkpoints sit after large-scale contrastive pretraining but before supervised finetuning on general retrieval, so they carry all the late-interaction structure with none of the general-purpose tuning that domain training then has to undo. The finished checkpoints, by contrast, barely moved or even regressed, at every learning rate I tried.

So, if the model family you like publishes a pre-supervised checkpoint, start there. If not, a fresh projection on a strong retrieval-pretrained backbone is a close runner-up. Continuing from a fully finished checkpoint is the weakest option for domain adaptation, despite being the most natural-feeling one.

The MultiVectorEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

According to recent reports, note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets on the Hub:.

In a recent development, this is the dataset I'll train on in this blogpost: 4.4 million medical questions from MIRIAD, each paired with the source passage that contains its answer (averaging 941 tokens). Simple (query, relevant passage) pairs like these are the easiest retrieval training data to collect for your own domain, and as you'll see, they're all you need.

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in common file formats:.

And if your local data requires pre-processing, you can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

According to recent reports, it is notable that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format). Verifying whether a dataset format works with a loss function involves two steps:.

There are two multi-vector specific conventions on top of this:.

It has been revealed that loss functions quantify how well a model performs for a given batch of data, allowing an optimizer to update the model weights to produce more favourable (i.e., lower) loss values. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of options in the Loss Overview.

For the common case of question-answer or question-passage pairs, the workhorse is in-batch negatives training with MultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, where every other document in the batch acts as a negative for each query. Bigger batches mean more negatives and stronger training, so in practice you'll want its GradCache variant, CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, which decouples the effective batch size from what fits on your GPU:.

Industry observers note that the mini_batch_size parameter bounds the memory by encoding documents in chunks of this size, while the effective contrastive batch size (128 in my run below, and in my ablations bigger batches bought nothing further) stays a free choice. GradCache guarantees identical results regardless of the chunk size, so lower it for smaller GPUs at only a wall-clock cost. When your document lengths vary a lot, consider its sibling mini_batch_num_tokens, which packs each chunk to a total token budget instead of a document count, so a chunk of unusually long documents can never spike your memory (my mini_batch_size=16 at roughly 940 tokens per document corresponds to mini_batch_num_tokens=15_000).

One multi-vector specific trap is that the contrastive losses default to scale=1.0, unlike the dense embedding equivalent which defaults to scale=20.0. That 20.0 exists because a cosine similarity is a single value in [-1, 1], too narrow a range for a sharp softmax. A MaxSim score instead sums one best-match similarity per query token, so it already spans roughly [0, query_length]: a 32-token query can score up to 32. So don't copy scale=20.0 over from a dense training script, since it would saturate the softmax and kill your gradients.

For distillation from a stronger teacher, which is how the strongest general-purpose late-interaction models are trained, see MultiVectorDistillKLDivLoss and the Knowledge Distillation tab in the Training Overview documentation.

You can customize the training process using the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

For more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Multi-Vector Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

To track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the trainer for evaluation loss, but concrete retrieval metrics are much more informative. Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators for multi-vector models:.

It has been revealed that for domain finetuning, the MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator built from your own held-out data is the one that matters. One tip on constructing it is that the corpus should be hard enough that models can be told apart. In my case the MIRIAD questions are generated from their own source passages, which makes retrieval unusually easy. Against just the 10k gold passages, nearly every model scored above 0.97 NDCG@10. If your evaluation saturates like that, add distractor passages (I use deduplicated passages from the training split) until the scores spread out:.

The MultiVectorEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. Here is the complete script that trained multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical, the model from the introduction:.

That's the whole recipe: a pre-supervised checkpoint, a million domain pairs, in-batch negatives, full document length, and a higher-than-usual learning rate. The run took 14.5 hours on my single RTX 3090 at a peak of 17.5 GB VRAM, and every one of those choices was the winner of a measured comparison rather than a guess.

Industry observers note that for readers on smaller budgets, my scaling experiments put 100k pairs (75 minutes of training) within 0.012 NDCG@10 of the full million-pair run. Most of the gain comes in the first hour.

The MultiVectorEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

In a recent development, enable these via the report_to training argument, e.g. report_to=["wandb", "codecarbon"], with the required dependencies installed. It defaults to "none", and report_to="all" activates every integration whose dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Sources indicate that typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the MultiVectorEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:.

Each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:.

To find out where the finetuned model stands, I evaluated it against over 50 retrieval model configurations across four architecture families on the MIRIAD evaluation set, built exactly as in the Evaluator section above, with 1,000 held-out medical questions searching 200,000 unique passages (the 10k gold passages hidden among 190k deduplicated distractors from the training split). This corpus is four times the size of the 50,000-passage one from Which starting point should you pick?, so scores are not comparable between the two tables.

The headline results, with the full table in the collapsible below:.

The finetuned model tops the table, beating the strongest zero-shot model of any architecture by +0.062 NDCG@10. In other words, the strongest zero-shot model returns the right passage as the very first hit for 75.8% of the queries, while the finetuned model does so for 84.9%, cutting the rank-1 error by more than a third.

Recent findings suggest that the architecture pattern is just as clear, with the top of the table exclusively late interaction. On long documents, one vector per token beats one vector per document, even at matched training and matched backbones. DenseOn and LateOn share training data and architecture except for the head, and the late-interaction sibling wins by +0.12, with the multilingual pair (mDenseOn and mLateOn) replicating this at +0.13. Scale doesn't rescue single vectors either. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest dense model with roughly 33x the active (non-embedding) parameters of mine, still stops 0.13 short, and the 8B version scores lower than the 4B.

BM25 also performs surprisingly well, beating every sparse model, every truncation-capped multi-vector model, and all but three dense models: the multi-billion Qwen3-Embedding-4B and 8B, and voyage-4-nano, which reads its full 32k token context to edge past by just 0.006. Don't expect that to transfer to your own data though. MIRIAD's questions are generated from the passages, so the lexical overlap between a query and its gold passage is far larger than in typical retrieval, and BM25's unlimited context length lets it use every one of those overlapping words while most neural checkpoints truncate. A BM25 baseline is cheap and always worth running, just don't count on this margin.

The full field at a glance, sorted by score and colored by architecture family.

In a recent development, models marked @N are evaluated with their document length cap lifted to N tokens, since their native caps (180 to 512 tokens) would otherwise truncate the 941-token average passages. For every multi-vector model this lift was worth +0.08 to +0.24 NDCG@10 over the as-served row, and even the dense DenseOn gained +0.03 from the same treatment.

Recent findings suggest that note that this does not mean that multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical is the strongest model on all domains. It's simply the strongest in my domain. This is totally fine, as I just need this model to work well on my data.

It has been revealed that don't underestimate the power of finetuning multi-vector models on your domain. Fourteen and a half hours on a single consumer GPU produced a model that no general-purpose retriever comes close to on this data, and the recipe is a single script with no teacher model and no mined negatives!

Industry observers note that the fair objection to multi-vector retrieval is index size, and this domain is close to the worst case for it. Storing one vector per token, my model needs about 878 vectors per passage, so the 200,000-passage corpus takes roughly 45 GB at fp16, where a dense model needs well under 1 GB. Document length is what makes that gap so wide. The Natural Questions passages in the companion post average about 125 token vectors each, seven times fewer, so a corpus of short passages starts from a far smaller index than this one does. The HierarchicalTokenPooling module compresses exactly this by clustering each document's token embeddings and storing the cluster means, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the vectors:.

I measured it post-hoc on the finished model, with no pooling-aware training, and on long documents it is remarkably cheap.

The solid points are uncompressed embeddings, so that every family is counted the same way and scored with exact search. You would not deploy any of them like that, though. Dense indexes routinely use int8 or binary quantization with rescoring, sparse indexes compress their postings, and multi-vector indexes use PLAID-style residual compression. Don't read those points as the disk you need to buy, but as relative storage cost.

In a recent development, token pooling is the solid line. Halving the vector count costs 0.0033 NDCG@10 and leaves rank-1 accuracy untouched, and keeping only a quarter of them, at 11.2 GB, still scores 0.8991. The curve keeps going (I measured out to a tenth of the vectors, still at 0.8765) but there is little reason to push pooling that far once quantization is on the table, which is what the dashed line below is about.

The dashed line is what a real deployment might look like. I gave Omar Khattab early access to the model and the benchmark, and he measured these configurations with fast-plaid at 1-bit residual quantization, using compact 17-bit centroid ids and 18-bit document ids instead of its ordinary unpacked 64-bit integers, plus document-side pruning:.

That first row is 13x smaller than the raw embeddings, for 0.0155 NDCG@10. That is a far better trade than anywhere on the pooling curve. Quantization shrinks each vector while pooling and pruning cut how many you keep, so they compose, and quantization is the one to reach for first. Push further and the last row lands at 1.45 GB, smaller than the fp16 embeddings of Qwen3-Embedding-8B (1.64 GB), while scoring 0.0895 higher. The objection that multi-vector indexes are too substantial does not survive a properly configured index.

The pruning here is naive, meant only to establish that token reduction works on top of quantization, so read the bottom two rows as a floor rather than the frontier. If you would rather not hand-tune quantization at all, the Indexing section of the companion post covers fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa.

Multi-vector retrieval is only as expensive as its index. The raw embeddings for this corpus are 45 GB, and a properly configured index is at least 7x smaller at nearly the same accuracy. The index deserves as much of your attention as the checkpoint.

Thanks to Omar Khattab for measuring the quantized and pruned index configurations in Optimizing the index, and for the discussions around late-interaction index costs.

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of playfy these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

Industry observers note that this is a really interesting deep dive into multi-vector embedding models... 🔥 The introduction of MultiVectorEncoder in Sentence Transformers v6.0 looks especially useful for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, where keeping multiple representations can capture much finer-grained matching than a single dense embedding. The fact that the same framework supports RAG, semantic search, and reranking makes this a very practical direction for modern retrieval systems. 🚀.

Industry observers note that I also like how the post breaks the finetuning process down into the individual pieces... datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. 🧠 Having practical examples around each component makes the approach much easier to understand and reproduce, especially for people who want to move beyond using a general-purpose retriever and actually optimize a model for their own domain.

It has been revealed that the medical retrieval results are probably the most impressive part... 💡 Training the mLateOn-medical multi-vector encoder for just 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 and getting better results than dense, sparse, lexical, and other multi-vector approaches shows how valuable domain-specific finetuning can be. It’s a great reminder that the biggest gains in retrieval often come from matching the model and training data closely to the actual search task rather than simply choosing the newest general-purpose model. 👏📚.

Overall, this is a great practical resource for anyone experimenting with advanced retrieval pipelines... ⚡ The ability to train strong multi-vector models from scratch as well as finetune existing ones opens up plenty of possibilities for specialized search and RAG applications. I especially appreciate that the whole workflow can be set up with sentence-transformers[train]... it makes an otherwise fairly complex retrieval training process feel much more approachable. 👍🤖.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.
  • VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 complications.
  • According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Four more critical vulns, including another unauthorized access flaw in vCenter.

VMware has issued its third critical security advisory in a week, this time to warn of four critical flaws and address a total of 23 complications.

According to recent reports, VMSA-2026-0011 landed on November 24, just five days after two other advisories. VMware’s FAQ for the newly introduced advisory includes the following remarks:.

Because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing this VMSA comes on the heels of VMSA-2026-0009, and atop a major holiday in the United States.The security vulnerability landscape is more dynamic than ever; please know that while we acknowledge this timing is not optimal, your ability to operate and maintain a secure environment amidst modern, AI-assisted threats is paramount to us.

Make of that what you will as you ponder how and when to patch the four critical flaws, including the 9.8-rated CVE-2026-123903, which allows a malicious actor to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to vCenter, the management tool VMware consumers rely on to manage hosts and VMs.

This is the third 9.8-rated authentication issue VMware has fixed in vCenter since July.

It has been revealed that two of the other critical flaws in this latest advisory allow an attacker to run code on an ESX host, earning the bugs a 9.8 rating. CVE-2026-123910 makes that possible thanks to a heap out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the I/O filter service, while CVE-2026-123911 is a use-after-free vulnerability.

The other critical flaw, CVE-2026-123912, can result in a guest escape from VMware’s desktop Workstation and Fusion desktop hypervisors. It’s also present in VMware’s ESX hypervisor, but attackers thankfully can’t escape that product’s sandbox. This one’s easy to mitigate because the problem is in a USB controller that consumers can turn off.

Most of the other flaws require installation of updated software.

There’s a little good news in that some of the software updates VMware issued last week include fixes for the newly disclosed flaws. But there are still plenty of fresh fixes to apply, across ten products: ESX, vCenter, Workstation, Fusion, VMware tools, Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, the Telco Cloud Platform, Telco Cloud Infrastructure, and the VMware Avi Load Balancer.

VMware’s advisory thanks external researchers for finding and reporting most of the flaws. The Broadcom business unit is known to be a member of Project Glasswing, the Anthropic-run effort to use the Mythos model to find flaws that has seen many vendors dramatically increase the number of patches they produce.

Sources indicate that in past years, VMware has often published considerably more than this year’s 11 security advisories. With five weeks left in the year, perhaps vAdmins need to worry Christmas might also get complicated. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a upcoming group of AWS Heroes. Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed. What they have in common is a genuine commitment to supporting the builders around them learn, grow, and lead.

Let us take a moment to meet them!

Industry observers note that serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder. On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make fresh technology easier to try. Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS.

In a recent development, community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI. Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days. At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders.

Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering. She leads the AWS User Group in Minas Gerais, hosts DataTalks Brasil, teaches MBA courses, and supports Women in Cloud, DevOpsDays, and AWS Community Day events. She speaks at events such as AWS Summit São Paulo and Web Summit Rio on database modernization and generative AI. At AWS re:Invent 2025, she was recognized as a LATAM Diversity & Inclusion Champion.

DevTools Hero Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka is an AWS CDK Top Contributor and Trusted CDK Community Reviewer. With 200 merged pull requests, he ranks 18th among more than 1,700 contributors. He has reviewed more than 120 pull requests, has been involved in about 2% of all CDK commits, and has published 10 construct libraries, along with tools such as cfn idle cost. Through talks at JAWS DAYS and CDK Conference Japan and through hands on contribution workshops, he helps more developers in Japan start contributing to open source.

To connect with these Heroes or find one in your region, explore the AWS Heroes webpage, and join the conversation on AWS Builder Center.

There’s recently been some discussion about the benefits and downsides of lock (mutex) poisoning in Rust, spurred by a recent proposal to make the default mutex non-poisoned, i.e. silently unlock on panic (see also, recent discussion on Hacker News). As a passionate defender of lock poisoning, I thought I’d gather and write about my thoughts on this matter.

According to recent reports, rust, like most multithreaded languages, has mutexes: a construct to ensure that a particular piece of data can only be accessed by one thread at a time. The way mutexes work in Rust is particularly well-considered:.

This is all quite reasonable! Let’s look at an example that processes incoming messages for a set of tracked operations. Let’s assume that multiple threads could be processing messages, so we have to guard the internal state with a mutex. (We’ll discuss alternative approaches to this problem later.).

This is a very typical use of mutexes: to guard one or more invariants or properties of some kind. These invariants are upheld while the mutex is unlocked. In this case, the invariant being guarded is that Operations::ops has complete and up-to-date tracking of all in-progress and completed operations.

According to recent reports, of equal importance is the fact that, while the mutex is held, the invariant is temporarily violated. In order to process the message, we have to remove the state from the map, create a fresh state, then put it back into the map. During this period, Operations::ops is missing this one operation, so it no longer tracks all operations. But this temporary violation is okay, because no other threads see this in-between state. Before the mutex is released, this code is responsible for putting the operation back into the map.

Is it always true that the operation is put back into the map? Unfortunately not always, in the presence of what I think of as unexpected errors. Many practitioners draw a separation between two different kinds of errors that a system can have. The terms recoverable and unrecoverable are sometimes used for them, but I tend to prefer the following terms (see also some discussion by Andrew Gallant):.

Sources indicate that generally, in Rust, expected errors are handled via the Result type, and unexpected errors are handled by panicking. Now, there isn’t a firm requirement that things be this way.

According to recent reports, but in typical production-grade Rust, expected errors are Results while unexpected errors (and only unexpected errors) are panics. Lock poisoning is built around this assumption.

In a recent development, consider what happens if a panic occurs in OperationState::process_message. This depends in part on the build flags and surrounding code, so let’s look closely at all the possibilities. In Rust, there are two ways to configure build flags on panic:.

In a recent development, some real-world applications (such as most of what we ship at Oxide) abort on panic, but most of this post is actually moot for aborts. So in the rest of this post, we’re going to focus on the default unwind behavior.

If a panic is invoked in the context of a catch_unwind, an Err(E) is returned, where the value E is whatever message or other payload the panic occurred with.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on the main thread, then a message is printed out and the program exits with an error.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

If there’s no catch_unwind, and the panic occurs on a different thread, then a message is printed out, and the panic message is returned as the result of JoinHandle::join.

If you run this slightly more complex program:.

and the program exits with a non-success exit code.

An interesting thing to note here is that there were two panics: one in the spawned child thread with the panic! message, and one in the main thread when the expect was called. The panic responsible for producing the non-success exit code was the one that occurred in the main thread, not the child thread.

This raises the question: what if a non-main thread panics and the thread is not joined? With this program:.

In a recent development, and the program exits with a successful exit code! There’s no indication that a panic occurred other than the message printed out, which can easily be missed.

Recent findings suggest that the upshot of all this is that panics in non-main threads are not magic. In order for the system to make decisions based on whether a panic occurred, it must process that, either with catch_unwind or via JoinHandle::join, and it’s all too easy to just ignore panics.

Coming back to our Operations example above, what does that mean for our mutex’s critical section?

This might look like a lot of ifs, but they’re more common than you might think: they’re all either the default in Rust or a very common way to write code.

Rust’s designers had the foresight to see this matter, and introduce lock poisoning as a detection mechanism for this failure mode. The way poisoning works is that:.

Almost all code immediately panics on seeing a PoisonError via .lock().unwrap(): this is often called propagating panics. But PoisonError can be handled more explicitly than that. Note that PoisonError, and poisoning more generally, is purely advisory: you can retrieve the data underneath, and even clear the poison bit in Rust 1.77 and above.

Recent findings suggest that the fact is, though, that anything other than .lock().unwrap() is rare in practice. This is emphatically not a reason to remove poisoning, and in fact is a strong argument to retain poisoning while making the ergonomics better (see below). What is vital is detection, not recovery.

It has been revealed that so, putting it all together: if a child thread panics in a critical section, then it is quite possible that the data is in an inconsistent or logically corrupt state. To indicate this, the mutex is marked poisoned. If the child thread is not waited on by the parent, this might be the only indication that a panic previously occurred in a critical section!

It is precisely this confluence of factors that makes lock poisoning such an important feature.

Industry observers note that is the problem of inconsistent mutex-guarded state limited to panic unwinding? I’d argue that it is a property of unexpected cancellations more generally: you start executing a critical section thinking that it will be run to completion, but something causes that process to be interrupted.

In Rust, there are two sources of unexpected cancellations, with strong parallels between them:.

Industry observers note that as documented in Oxide RFD 397 and RFD 400, unexpected future cancellations have resulted in so many mutex invariant violations that we now avoid Tokio mutexes entirely1. My perspective here comes from much pain dealing with this concern in async Rust, and wanting very much for this footgun to not make its way to synchronous Rust.

See the appendix for more details.

In other words, is poisoning often too conservative? My answer to this is that panics do not always cause invariant violations, but they’re so common, and the downsides of corrupt state so unbounded, that it is still valuable to have lock poisoning as a strong heuristic.

Firstly, if all you’re doing is reading data that just happens to be guarded by a mutex (maybe because some other function writes to that data), a panic in the critical section can’t cause invariant violations. (But also, you may wish to use an RwLock.).

In a recent development, secondly, some simple kinds of writes can also avoid causing invariant violations. For example if all you’re doing is updating some counters2:.

Finally, it is sometimes possible to carefully architect code to be unwind safe, such that if a panic occurs, either:.

In a recent development, for example, the standard library’s HashMap and BTreeMap are architected this way. In our Operations example, we could, rather than removing the operation from the map entirely, replace it with an Invalid sentinel state.

In these cases, it is true that a panic in a critical section is not harmful, and that the typical .lock().unwrap() approach will reduce system availability. But the key thing to keep in mind is that code changes over time. One of the things I like about Rust is how resilient it is to changes over time: by encoding properties like mutable access into the type system, Rust makes it that much harder for latest team members (or even yourself six months from now) to screw up. However, like async cancel safety, unwind safety is not encoded in Rust’s type system3, so it’s easy for code that’s fine today to be wrong tomorrow.

It has been revealed that the main downside to a .lock().unwrap() that misfires is reduced availability and denial of service. But the downsides to an undetected panic are unbounded, and can range from denial of service all the way to “(part of) an HTTP request ending up sent to a party it should not have been sent to,” or in other words personal information leakage.

A downside that (while potentially serious) is bounded, versus the kind of flaw that can kill an organization—I know which default I want.

What about writing panic-free code? You can carefully write your critical sections to not have panics. But that is a property that’s especially hard to maintain as code changes over time. Even something as simple as a println! can panic. Also, if the critical section can’t panic, then it doesn’t matter whether the mutex poisons or not.

A bit of history here: in Rust 1.0, panics could only be detected at thread boundaries via JoinHandle::join. This meant that back then, the only way for panics to cause invariant violations was for:.

Since then, two Rust features were added:.

Recent findings suggest that with both of these, you can operate on arbitrary data (i.e. not just data guarded by a mutex) and leave it in an inconsistent state. To see how, let’s rewrite the Operations example above to not have a mutex inside of it, and to require exclusive access to make any modifications to it.

Recent findings suggest that since there are no mutexes involved any more, this is no longer a critical section in the classical sense. But note that we still have the invariant that ops tracks all operations. This invariant is temporarily violated, with the idea that it’ll be restored before the function returns. Since &mut means nothing else has any kind of access (read or write) to this data, we know that this in-between state is not seen by anybody else.

Sources indicate that but just like with mutexes, this breaks down with unwinding. With catch_unwind, you can do:.

And with scoped threads, you can do:.

Sources indicate that if a panic occurs in process_message, Operations is logically corrupted. This failure mode has resulted in a proposal to have a Poison wrapper that poisons on panicking. That absolutely makes sense and is worth pursuing.

Sources indicate that but, along with the Poison wrapper, there are some suggestions to go further and suggest that the current std::sync::Mutex type should be changed in the next Rust edition to, instead of poisoning on panic, silently unlock. (And also, as a followup, that the current Mutex should instead become Mutex>.).

(It’s worth noting that there’s another non-poisoning option: the mutex stays locked forever, as C programmers might expect. This option is somewhat appealing because it is safe by default, in a sense. But once a thread is stuck waiting on the mutex, there’s no easy way to recover. So it’s not panics that propagate, it’s stuck threads. This seems strictly worse than a poisoning mutex to me, so I’ll assume the proposal means silent unlocking.).

I first want to give credit to this proposal: it is quite beautiful.

While all of these are true, I keep coming back to how unbounded the downside of an undetected panic is, and how easy it is to get wedged in this state. Mutexes and poisoning have value separate from each other, but I don’t think they are as independent as they seem at first. My understanding from writing Rust code over many years is that almost all uses of mutexes benefit from poisoning, and almost all instances of poisoning one needs to care about are with mutex-guarded data.

Why are mutexes special? As we’ve established above, poisoning can make sense in non-mutex contexts too. What makes mutexes a particularly valuable place to have it? The reason has to do with what I like to call the cancellation blast radius. Corrupted data only matters if it is shared mutable state: changed in a way that resulted in an invariant violation, and visible outside of where the failure occurred. If a typical &mut reference panics in the middle of an operation, it’s likely that the data it is referring to will also be torn down, in which case those invariant violations don’t matter4. But the whole point of mutexes is that they’re shared across threads! So data corruption is almost certain to be externally visible.

There are some use cases that would benefit from non-poisoning mutexes, like metrics and best-effort logging, but those cases shouldn’t drive the default.

It has been revealed that more specifically, I am worried that a common complaint about lock poisoning (see below) is that it has too much friction. Having to use Mutex> instead of Mutex adds even more friction, so people are going to opt for non-poisoning mutexes more of the time. This is going to lead to grave mistakes in production.

In a recent development, this is a spot where zero-cost abstractions and safety by default are seemingly at odds with each other. I would like to see performance numbers to quantify this better, but if I may hazard a guess, the incremental cost of checking the poison flag (a single atomic load with relaxed ordering) is minimal compared to the cost of acquiring the lock in the first place.

I mentioned earlier that parking_lot’s mutexes silently unlock on panic. A large chunk of the Rust ecosystem uses parking_lot today, often for performance reasons. Does that mean that code using parking_lot has these unbounded downsides?

The answer depends on a bunch of things, but in general (and especially in library code) that is indeed what I’m suggesting. For instance, this critical section in parity-db is quite large. Reasoning about whether it’s unwind-safe seems very difficult to me; this is exactly the kind of code that mutex poisoning does well to guard against.

In this case, the binary is configured to abort on panic, so it’s fine. But reusable Rust libraries cannot require panic = 'abort', and if this code were in a library on crates.io, it would be a real cause for concern.

Industry observers note that A common response to this class of issue is to not bother with any of this unwinding stuff, and always abort on panic. This comes back to the idea of the cancellation blast radius described above: aborting the process on panic guarantees that in-memory state is torn down.

I have a lot of sympathy for this idea! This is what we do at Oxide. (Why am I writing this post if it doesn’t affect my workplace? Well, first, I care about the health of Rust more generally. Second, libraries must work with unwinds. But most importantly, we have seen the pain of unexpected async cancellations at Oxide, so we know how bad it can be.).

It has been revealed that but also, that works fine with the current approach: .lock().unwrap() always succeeds. Whether mutexes poison or not only matters with panic = 'unwind'.

This leads to what I think is driving a lot of discussion here:.

Recent findings suggest that I get this complaint. I really do. Having to write .lock().unwrap() everywhere sucks. It’s extra characters in a language already filled with syntax noise. It can cause rustfmt to format your line of code across multiple lines.

Industry observers note that these are all valid points. But there is a much better solution for them, one that doesn’t give up the very notable benefits of poisoning: in the next Rust edition, make lock() automatically panic if the mutex is poisoned! (And add a lock_or_poison method for the current behavior5).

It’s worth comparing the different options here:.

Based on this table, I believe the answer is clear: if a breaking change is going to happen, it’s much better to make lock automatically panic than to make panics silently unlock.

According to recent reports, concurrent programming is very difficult. Rust makes it easier than most other languages, and lock poisoning is an important part of the story. Let’s avoid introducing any regressions here.

Recent findings suggest that providing a Poison wrapper makes a lot of sense. Making the default std::sync::Mutex silently unlock on panic would, however, be a mistake.

Should Rust’s standard library even provide non-poisoning mutexes? That’s a harder question. I’m worried that their mere presence in the standard library will lower the barrier to people doing the wrong thing, particularly in libraries where panic = 'abort' cannot be assumed. But I think non-poisoning mutexes have some legitimate uses, so I don’t object too strenuously if the tradeoffs are carefully documented.

Writing all this out was very helpful to me in getting my thoughts straight, and I hope it’s helpful to you too.

Updated 2025-12-06: Added a section to Separating mutexes from poisoning on what makes poisoning particularly valuable for mutexes, more than in other contexts.

Recent findings suggest that unlike panics, the standard library’s mutex does not poison on future cancellations. (I believe it’s not possible to poison on future cancellations with the RAII pattern.).

Sources indicate that but wait! Tokio provides its own Mutex type, which is sendable to another thread. This means that it is possible to put an await point in a critical section, and so the matter of unexpected cancellations within a critical section rears its ugly head with Tokio mutexes.

Tokio mutexes also do not poison if the critical section panics. At Oxide we abort on panic so this matters less as a reason to avoid them, but is yet another asterisk that pushes me away from them. ↩︎.

A more typical way to manage simple counters is with an atomic, but if the data is more complex than just an integer, a mutex may be necessary. ↩︎.

Rust does have some rudimentary support for unwind safety in the type system, but it is more of a suggestion that most users ignore, and because of that there’s a proposal to remove it from Rust. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that the exception is Drop implementations, which may have to be written robustly to guard against temporary invariant violations. ↩︎.

The more obvious try_lock is already taken. ↩︎.
