#207136. The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2472 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The Open ASR Leaderboard Adds Its First Global South Language

📅 28 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.
  • A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve.
  • Sources indicate that all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice Arena and Hugging Face partner to launch open ASR evaluation for Hindi and Indian English.

Benchmarks decide what gets built. A model that scores well on the Open ASR Leaderboard gets adopted and iterated on, while capabilities the leaderboard does not measure tend not to improve. Much of the recent work on the leaderboard has gone into making the evaluation metrics more trustworthy:.

Sources indicate that all of that makes one number (WER) harder to game. It is still one number. A long line of work has shown that ASR error rates are not evenly distributed across the people using them. Racial disparities in automated speech recognition found commercial systems roughly twice as bad for Black speakers as for white speakers, and Quantifying Bias in Automatic Speech Recognition found further differences by gender, age and accent. None of that is visible on a leaderboard, and not because the leaderboard is hiding it. The test sets it runs on record what was said and almost nothing about who said it.

To address this gap, we introduce two evaluation sets to the Open ASR Leaderboard: Monsoon en-IN and Monsoon hi-IN. Hindi, spoken by more than half a billion people, is the first Indic language on a multilingual tab that right now covers only European languages. Each set is released as a public split, available for self-scoring, and a private split withheld to limit benchmark-specific optimisation. The four splits are speaker-disjoint, comprising 4,888 speakers, with 12 speaker attributes recorded for each.

A test set can only expose a failure mode it varies along. Most benchmarks are built from whatever audio was readily available. Monsoon was built to vary along nine axes: geography, age, gender, vocabulary, devices, acoustic environments, speech type, speech rate, and the existence of multiple valid transcripts for the same audio. Each is a way an aggregate WER can be right on average and wrong for a particular population.

The collection method follows from that.

Four splits, two languages, collected through one pipeline.

The data is sourced from unscripted dual-channel spontaneous conversations, with clips segmented from a single channel so that each clip carries one speaker. Along with the fields reported in the table, each clip also records occupation, education, marital status, income band, handset brand, current city and years in the current district.

Five clips from the public Indian English split, with the metadata each one carries:.

29-year-old woman, West Tripura, Tripura. Student, samsung SM-G781B.

32-year-old woman, Satna, Madhya Pradesh. Unemployed, samsung SM-E146B.

22-year-old man, Rohtas, Bihar. Student, motorola moto g54 5G.

Sources indicate that 27-year-old woman, Warangal, Telangana. Unemployed, vivo V2247.

In a recent development, 57-year-old man, Puducherry. Private job, Xiaomi M2006C3LI.

Sources indicate that the English sets use standard string references, where the leaderboard's normaliser collapses most spelling variation. Hindi has far more of it, and no normaliser can resolve it, because the variants are not a fixed mapping between two conventions. The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, a list of the spellings that are accepted as correct.

Monsoon is small measured in hours and large measured in speakers. That is the design, and it is where most of the value sits.

Speaker concentration and diversity beyond the fields above.

Three properties follow, and each is a claim about variance rather than volume.

No voice carries the score: The ten largest contributors account for between 2.8% and 6.8% of total duration, and more than half of all speakers appear exactly once. A result on Monsoon is an average over hundreds of distinct voices, not a small number of talkers recorded at length. Test sets of comparable duration are usually constructed the other way.

It has been revealed that no region or handset carries it either: The Indian English public set draws on 428 native districts across 30 states and union territories; the Hindi sets, being a Hindi-belt language, concentrate more tightly but still span 202 and 295 districts. Recordings come from 315 to 582 distinct device models, with no single model exceeding 2.1% of segments in any subset. Corpora collected on standardised hardware overfit to one microphone response; this one cannot.

According to recent reports, indian English here is not one accent: This is English as it is spoken across the country, not the English of one region. All six zones are represented: in the public set, 35% of segments are contributed by southern speakers, 18% from the East, 18% from Central, 16% from the North and 11% from the West. The accent variation that follows from that spread is recorded in the metadata rather than asserted.

In a recent development, monsoon ships 18 columns per segment, of which 12 are metadata, where most public ASR test sets ship an identifier, a transcript and a duration. Demographic fields are complete or near-complete; contributors consented to this use.

The two languages have different geographic shapes, and the shape is informative. The Hindi sets concentrate in the Hindi belt, with Uttar Pradesh accounting for roughly 40% of speakers, which is what a Hindi corpus sampled by population should look like. The Indian English sets are much flatter: no state exceeds 13%, and a third of speakers come from outside the eight largest. Public and private halves match closely on both.

Indian state boundaries were drawn along linguistic lines, so district and state carry real accent signal, which is why these fields are released rather than summarised away. Analysis of this kind has been reported at scale for Indian ASR: district-level error rates spanning roughly 4% to 44%, with underrepresented regions well behind the Hindi belt and the metros, plus disaggregation by audio quality, speaking rate, utterance duration, gender, age and device. Those runs were on a closed benchmark. Monsoon makes the same class of analysis possible on a public leaderboard test set.

Broad geographic coverage requires recruitment across hundreds of districts rather than longer sessions from fewer speakers, and distributed recruitment at this scale introduces failure modes that a smaller collection does not face: contributors gaming the task, played-back audio submitted as live speech, and inattentive annotation. Each is addressed by an explicit check.

In a recent development, recruitment and recording: Contributors were recruited through the Voice Arena community, a global digital platform whose reach extends into the rural and semi-urban districts that speech corpora rarely cover. Pairs then recorded two-person conversations over a peer-to-peer interface, dual-channel, on assigned everyday topics. Contributors used their own handsets and their own connections. Many of those are low-end devices on unstable bandwidth, which is why that condition is present in the released audio rather than filtered out of it. Prospective contributors completed a language proficiency screening before being granted recording access, were compensated, and provided informed consent covering use in training and distribution. A per-speaker duration cap, calibrated per language to the population size and geographic distribution of its speakers, prevented a small number of prolific contributors from dominating a language or region; more than half of the speakers in these sets contribute exactly one segment.

Industry observers note that elicitation: Eliciting spontaneous speech at scale presents its own difficulty, as contributors tend to produce short and sparse responses without structured guidance. Each conversation was therefore seeded with an open-ended narrative cue and progressively revealed follow-up questions, spanning domains including travel, healthcare, agriculture, education and digital services, guiding the exchange toward extended description without scripting it. Candidate topics were generated with large language models, then reviewed and localised by native-speaker linguists.

It has been revealed that quality control: Every recording passed a set of gating checks prior to transcription. The spoken language was verified against the assigned language using language identification models trained on human-annotated data across more than 30 languages. Speaker gender was confirmed against the self-reported label using a dedicated classifier, applied as corroboration of the self-report rather than as a replacement for it. A further model distinguished genuine spontaneous conversation from pre-recorded or played-back audio. Signal-to-noise ratio estimation removed recordings degraded beyond intelligibility, while natural environmental background noise was deliberately preserved so that the acoustic realism of in-the-wild speech is retained. Recordings clearing these checks were segmented by voice activity detection, split at two seconds of continuous silence or at a fifteen-second soft cap closed at the next detected silence. Segmentation was applied independently per channel, so every segment is single-speaker and single-channel. Segments then passed a DNSMOS P.808 check.

Industry observers note that transcription: Reference transcripts are human work. A first draft was generated by internal ASR models trained on in-domain data, none of which appear on any public leaderboard, so no system evaluated on these sets contributed to the references it is scored against. Every subsequent stage was performed by native-speaking linguists under a five-level protocol built on a strict separation of labour, in which each correction round is followed by an independent verification round performed by a different annotator, so no linguist audits their own output. A linguist first corrects the draft segment by segment against the acoustic signal; a second re-verifies it and flags residual disagreements. Subsequent levels iterate this cycle with fresh annotators, progressively resolving ambiguous phonetic realisations, code-switching boundaries, named entities, and orthographic consistency across spelling variants. Numerals are written as words, so that the transcript corresponds directly to what was spoken. Segments still flagged at the final level were returned for re-transcription before admission. Annotator behaviour was monitored automatically throughout, flagging submissions containing characters outside the target script, unnatural character or word repetitions, and unusually low or high edit counts.

In a recent development, what follows is one example, run on the public Indian English split, to show the kind of evaluation the metadata makes possible. It is not the finding the sets exist to deliver; it is an illustration of what becomes answerable once every clip carries a speaker.

Eight models on the leaderboard land between 4.81 and 4.99 WER on this set. That is 0.18 points from best to worst, inside what five hours can resolve. Ranked on the corpus, they are the same model.

Grouping speakers by region tells a different story. Each speaker's native district is rolled up to its zonal council, the Ministry of Home Affairs grouping of Indian states, giving five well-sampled zones. openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo varies by 0.46 points across them. mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507, fourteen hundredths of a point behind it on the corpus, varies by 1.68, running 4.38 in the Central zone against 6.06 in the East. Two systems that are indistinguishable on the leaderboard differ almost fourfold in how much their accuracy depends on where the speaker is from.

It has been revealed that which zone is hardest is not fixed either. ibm-granite/granite-speech-3.3-2b is worst in the North, microsoft/VibeVoice-ASR-HF in the South, mistralai/Voxtral-Mini-3B-2507 in the East. If a single region were simply harder to transcribe, every model would rank the zones the same way. They do not, which points at the models rather than the audio.

Sources indicate that region is one of twelve recorded attributes, and the zones above are a coarse rollup of 428 districts. The same breakdown runs on age, education, occupation and handset, and the released files carry everything needed to reproduce it. None of it is available for a test set that records only what was said.

In a recent development, english orthographic variation is bounded. British against American spelling, punctuation, casing, digits against words: a normaliser can map most of it to a single form, and the leaderboard's does. Hindi is not bounded in the same way. Everyday speech is heavily code-mixed, English-origin words have no settled Devanagari spelling, and compound forms are written joined or separated according to preference. A single phrase can have ten or more valid written forms, and no fixed mapping collapses them, because there is no canonical side to map to.

Industry observers note that scored with a single reference, WER rewards a system for producing the spelling the annotator happened to choose. Two systems that recognised the audio equally well can differ by several points on orthography alone.

The Hindi sets therefore ship a lattice: for each span of the transcript, the set of written forms accepted as correct. Building it is manual work. Candidate variants are drawn from multiple ASR transcripts of the same audio and expanded with language models, then native-speaker linguists decide which are valid for that utterance and prune the rest, so only forms consistent with what was said are admitted.

Recent findings suggest that thus, for Hindi we report the Orthographically-Informed Word Error Rate (OIWER), introduced by AI4Bharat, instead of WER. A hypothesis is aligned against the accepted set at each span, so any admitted form counts as correct and only genuine recognition errors are charged.

In a recent development, to quantify the effect, the same hypotheses were scored twice. Flattening each lattice to its first variant per span yields a single string reference of the kind a conventional benchmark provides; any of the admitted variants would serve equally well, and a different choice would yield a different reference. Scored against the flattened reference, error rates rise for every system, and they do not rise uniformly. Rankings change as a consequence. The figure below reveals two pairs of systems that reverse order between the two references: under a single reference a system is rewarded in part for reproducing the annotator's orthography, whereas the lattice scores only recognition.

We also open source our implementation, voi-oiwer, so every result on these sets can be reproduced directly.

For the private splits, get your model on the Open ASR Leaderboard and the Hugging Face team will run the evaluation. As before, the process for adding a model to the leaderboard takes place on the Open ASR Leaderboard GitHub:.

Indian-English joins the main leaderboard as Voice Arena Monsoon, in the default column set rather than as an opt-in toggle, so it contributes to the headline Average WER for every model. The private split feeds the aggregated Private (conversational) column alongside Appen and DataoceanAI data. The public and private Hindi appears in the Multilingual tab, where a model is ranked only if it supports every selected language, making that column a like-for-like comparison. Alternative, select "Hindi" from the "Language dataset breakdown" dropdown menu.

Hindi is a sharp case of a general problem. Any language written more than one way, spoken by people a benchmark has not sampled, carries both of the failures described here. These sets do not fix them. What they add is a way to see them: a test set on a leaderboard the field already watches, carrying enough about each speaker and each reference that a difference between two systems can be traced to who was talking and how they write it, instead of disappearing into one number.

These four sets are part of Monsoon, Voice Arena's broader dataset initiative for the Global South.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.
  • A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.
  • Recent findings suggest that this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Criminal masterminds claimed to work for ‘Weihua’ or to have source code from ‘oscic’ instead of Cisco.

A US jury has found Chinese tech giant Huawei stole tech from American companies, laundered money, and violated sanctions by building major internet infrastructure for Iran, but didn’t operate an illegal racket to get that done.

Recent findings suggest that this case kicked off in 2020, when the US Department of Justice claimed entities Huawei operated in America violated federal law. The indictment led to a trial on a dozen criminal matters that has played out over the last three months in the Eastern District Court of New York.

The trial ended on Tuesday when a jury found Huawei and three subsidiary companies guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, conspiracy to commit wire and bank fraud, wire fraud, bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the United States, conspiracy to violate the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) and substantive violations of that law, plus money laundering conspiracy.

The Department of Justice’s celebration of the decision indicates Huawei was found to have stolen Cisco’s source code, after prosecutors highlighted evidence that “Huawei engineers left Cisco’s notes about the Cisco code, referred to Cisco using its name backwards ‘ocsic’ and described that portions of the code remained as they existed in the ‘ocsic’ code.”.

Another item of evidence apparently highlighted a Huawei staffer photographing Fujitsu equipment while wearing a fake employee badge for a organization called “Weihua” – cunningly reversing the two syllables of “Huawei.”.

Another allegation the jury accepted involved Huawei staffers signing a non-disclosure agreement (NDA) ahead of a visit to T-Mobile to inspect a robot the telco created to test mobile devices.

Recent findings suggest that huawei staff ignored that NDA so thoroughly that they “sent photographs and technical details of the robot back to China” so the Chinese company could make its own robot. “When that data was not sufficient, a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DoJ states.

Recent findings suggest that the feds say the Chinese company also “lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of U.S. dollars and access to U.S.-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”.

Huawei has issued a statement noting that the jury found it not guilty of racketeering and insisting the charges on which it was found guilty are “without legal or factual merit.”.

“The five trade secret-related disputes cited by the government were all civil matters that were resolved over the past two decades,” the statement adds.

Sentencing will take place in September 2027.

The presiding judge will likely consider the fact that in 2017, US authorities fined Chinese telco equipment maker ZTE $900 million just for selling to Iran, then added an additional $1.4 billion penalty to lift a ban on doing business in the USA.

Washington has already banned Huawei from selling its telco products and personal devices in the USA. Lawmakers have little appetite to let the Chinese company return to the American market after spending billions to help American telcos replace the Huawei kit with locally made alternatives. ®.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2081 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI).
  • Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless.
  • It has been revealed that cost is the second problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

It has been revealed that cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:.

Industry observers note that part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

It has been revealed that first, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

In a recent development, the Lambda console indicates the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:.

It has been revealed that after pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

It has been revealed that GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview indicates what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Industry observers note that functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Sources indicate that then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

It has been revealed that four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

Sources indicate that that’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a fresh version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

Industry observers note that for production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab reveals the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

Sources indicate that no GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Industry observers note that trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

In a recent development, serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Sources indicate that multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

Recent findings suggest that see GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

Sources indicate that after invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

October in Servo: video captions and inert content

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Servo

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a newly introduced record)!
  • Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!
  • Flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plus WebAudio nodes, image inputs, and more!

Servo 0.8.0 contains all of the changes we landed in October, spanning 588 commits (a newly introduced record)!

Servo now renders subtitles and captions over elements (@TimvdLippe, #48809)!

We’ve shipped latest web platform features:.

Flutter web content no longer hangs now that we fixed a serious performance problem with typed arrays (@jdm, #48640). Example.

It has been revealed that we’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub concerns.

Recent findings suggest that with respect to accessibility in Servo, we report many more ARIA roles for DOM elements (@alice, @mrobinson, #48839). These can be inspected with the Get Computed Role WebDriver command (@lolaodelola, #47339). Accessibility integration can be turned on with the accessibility_enabled preference.

Sources indicate that webGL2 support received lots of attention this month, with fixes to getParameter(), drawBuffers(), readBuffers(), vertexAttribIPointer(), DEPTH_STENCIL_ATTACHMENT, getUniformLocation(), vertexAttrib4x(), pixelStorei(), texStorage2D(), texStorage3D(), texImage3D(), getInternalformatParameter(), blitFramebuffer(), and texSubImage2D() (@mxmgorin, #48651, #48620, #48678, #48689, #48751, #48681, #48911, #48972, #48590, #49201, #49289, #48560, #48571). The feature remains gated behind the dom_webgl2_enabled preference.

Reading and writing mapped WebGPU buffers got a significant speed increase (@sagudev, @jdm, #48372). WebGPU can be enabled with the dom_webgpu_enabled preference.

Industry observers note that JS script compilation can now occur off the main thread when the dom_script_asynch preference is enabled (@Gae24, #45687). Right now this only applies to non-module scripts.

Initial support for the backdrop-filter property has merged (@shubhamg13, #48829). This can be enabled with the layout_css_backdrop_filter_enabled preference.

ServiceWorkers now fire the statechange event when changing states during initialization (@gterzian, #48749). ServiceWorkerContainer can listen for message and messageerror events (@gterzian, #48680). Service Workers remain gated behind the dom_serviceworker_enabled preference.

According to recent reports, the Geolocation API has been implemented (@webbeef, #48406). No platform-specific backends to provide the device geolocation data have merged yet, so it remains disabled behind the dom_geolocation_enabled preference.

DOM interfaces for MathML elements now exist, gated behind the mathml_core_enabled preference (@tannal, #48631). There is no MathML-specific layout implemented yet.

A new, native SVG implementation is in progress (@mu-mostafa98, @jdm, #48467). This work is still in the early stages, but is intended to replace Servo’s dependency on the resvg crate to better integrate with page styling and animations.

Recent findings suggest that indexedDB cursors now support the enhancement() and delete() methods (@kuntal-devrat, #48402). The feature can be enabled with the dom_indexeddb_enabled preference.

Support for LargestContentfulPaint performance timing improved, with image URLs (@shubhamg13, #48668), the loadTime value (@shubhamg13, #48676), ignoring non-paintable elements (@shubhamg13, #48856, #48898), video URLs (@shubhamg13, #48931), and following containing blocks (@shubhamg13, #48551). This work is behind the largest_contentful_paint_enabled preference.

It has been revealed that we added support for a latest performance timing metric: ContainerTiming (@jasonwilliams, #46966). This can be enabled with the container_timing_enabled preference.

Recent findings suggest that our support for adoptedStylesheets improved along with a new implementation of the ObservableArray specification concept (@jerensl, @arihant2math, #48506). This is currently hidden behind the dom_adoptedstylesheet_enabled preference.

The Android Compose migration is complete, and embedders now only need to interact with the Servo library component (@veyndan, #48592, #48601, #48595, #48574, #48609, #48778, #48780, #49266). Embedders no longer need to trigger the soft keyboard display; this is controlled by a parameter to the Servo component (@veyndan, #48757).

There’s a new API method to report the network status of the embedder: NetworkManager::set_online_state (@xbwwj, #47568). This data is exposed via the onLine property of the Navigator interface in web content.

Industry observers note that embedders can now disable all support for developer tools, which can reduce the size of the final binary (@janeoa, #47255). This is controlled by the devtools feature and enabled by default; it is also part of the new default_tooling feature.

Users of the C API can set preferences that accept f64 and f64 array parameters (@fran6co, #49325), as well as the HiDPI scale factor for each WebView (@fran6co, #49327). WebViews can also be resized via the C API (@fran6co, #49326).

In a recent development, the layout_grid_enabled preference has been removed, since CSS Grid now defaults to enabled (@Loirooriol, #48718). Several preferences were renamed (@nicoburns, #48915):.

Double and triple clicking on selected text will extend the selection to the current word and line, respectively (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #48767).

Clicking a link with the middle mouse button now opens up the link in a new WebView (@SteveSharonSam, @mrobinson, #46000).

Range inputs can be dragged with the mouse (@webbeef, #48342).

Command+delete on macOS will delete the preceding line in a text control (@dzfrias, #48781).

The developer tools continue to improve:.

We improved exception error messages related to the XMLHttpRequest, History, Range, Selection, Element, CharacterData, and DOMTokenList interfaces, and namespaces and attributes (@gabrielecabrini, #49146, #49145, #48786, #49102).

Media elements that start playing outside of a document will no longer be garbage collected until playback finishes (@sabbCodes, @jdm, #49367, #48979).

Pinch zoom operations no longer have to rebuild a full display list, making zooming complex pages much smoother (@stevennovaryo, @mrobinson, #43561).

It has been revealed that we improved performance in many small and focused ways by doing less work during restyling and layout (@SimonSapin, @webbeef, @nicoburns, @mrobinson, #49137, #49100, #48485, #48968), reducing GC interactions (@mrobinson, @jschwe, #48984, #49140, #49195, #49425), and delaying work on disconnected trees (@SimonSapin, #49098). We also fixed instances of quadratic layout with deep nesting (@nicoburns, #49148) and missing caching (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #49164, #49073).

We fixed some intermittent GC panics when notifying ResizeObservers (@mrobinson, #49189), introspecting keyframes (@MohamedAli00949, #48546), setting timers (@jdm, #48548), using writable streams (@jdm, #48656), and scrolling iframes after removing them (@mrobinson, #49230).

We also fixed numerous other panics and crashes in scrollable and incremental layout (@mrobinson, #49230, #49283), moving nodes around (@mrobinson, #49226), using WebGPU from opaque origins (@gabrielecabrini, #49207), stringifying some WebIDL types (@mrobinson, #49374), using readable streams (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #49311), clicking disabled file controls (@mrobinson, #49379), rendering giant SVGs (@sabbCodes, #49264), unminifying JS (@jdm, #48567), measuring text (@mxmgorin, #48621), rendering text tracks (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48827), preparing dialogs (@lukewarlow, #49431), and running delayed tasks in destroyed documents (@mrobinson, @jdm, #49399, #48714).

Many small-to-medium improvements to reduce allocations were merged (@yezhizhen, @Narfinger, @Taym95, @mrobinson, @Loirooriol, @CynthiaOketch, @sabbCodes, @mxmgorin, #48549, #48558, #48568, #48598, #48615, #48565, #48646, #48654, #48569, #48562, #48588, #48650, #48702, #48675, #48589, #48720, #48721, #47720, #48745, #48703, #48750, #48770, #48789, #48754, #48828, #48838, #48836, #48841, #48843, #48867, #48882, #48842, #48881, #48840, #48899, #48924, #48904, #48949, #48953, #48980, #49028, #48885, #49035, #49038, #49084, #49131, #49125, #48951, #49154, #49160, #49198, #49202, #49194, #49219, #49258, #49275, #49295, #49298, #49300, #49320, #49323, #49313, #49373, #49380, #48969, #48991). We also reduced memory usage by shrinking some types (@Narfinger, @webbeef, #48954, #48082, #48906).

Memory leaks received a lot of attention this month, covering everything from network requests, to JS modules, to timer tasks, and more (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, @jschwe, #48952, #48957, #49032, #49049, #49092, #49134, #49139, #49132, #48747, #48752).

We continue to work towards preventing certain sources of memory leaks with static analysis and the Rust type system (@Gae24, @Narfinger, @jdm, #48147, #48360, #48832, #48887, #48913, #48903, #48965, #48905, #48834, #48855, #49083, #49082, #49081, #49096, #49135, #49130).

We fixed bugs related to the CORS preflight cache (@sabbCodes, #49055, #49252), fetch metadata (@TimvdLippe, @mrobinson, #48793), HTTP cache revalidation (@mrobinson, @jdm, #48927), image load timing (@mrobinson, @TimvdLippe, #48902, #48790, #48599), touch events (@yezhizhen, #48671, #48699, #48701), cloning and moving input elements (@skyz1, @mrobinson, #48845, #48069), the :indeterminate pseudoclass (@skyz1, #48070), stylesheet introspection (@mrobinson, #48935), mutating ranges (@gabrielecabrini, #49072), blob URLs (@rogerkorantenng, #49074, #48989, #49206), form controls (@mrobinson, @lukewarlow, @jdm, #49163, #49225, #48513), the mapping property of Gamepad (@msub2, #49381), beforeinput events (@dzfrias, #48825), image dimensions (@TimvdLippe, #49085), table appearance attributes (@Loirooriol, #49120, #49108, #49156, #49150), IME events (@dzfrias, #48690), reconnecting IntersectionObserver (@shubhamg13, #48581), and root elements (@TimvdLippe, #48514).

We also addressed layout issues related to soft wrap line breaks (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48564), grid and flex layouts with indefinite dimensions (@RichardTjokroutomo, @rayguo17, @nicoburns, #48670, #48644, #49232), hanging whitespace (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48591, #48753), preserve-3d (@mrobinson, #47933), inline block splits (@Loirooriol, #46445), video controls (@rayguo17, #44956), display: contents (@Loirooriol, #48784, #48785), justify-contents (@yezhizhen, #48746, #48988), absolute positioning (@mrobinson, @Loirooriol, #48846), (@Loirooriol, #49143), text-transform: capitalize (@jschwe, #48901), incremental table layout (@Loirooriol, #49176), width: stretch (@Loirooriol, #49239, #49237), backface visibility (@mrobinson, #49196), flex gaps (@yezhizhen, #49335), perspective (@mrobinson, #49174), quirks mode (@Loirooriol, #48942, #39869, #48978, #49211), SVG viewboxes (@leowatts, #48556), ISO-8859-8 documents (@TTyChud, #48444), and table borders (@adoublebarrel, @mrobinson, #47684).

A special thanks to the following people for landing their first patch in Servo:.

Interested in helping build a web browser? Take a look at our curated list of problems that are good for upcoming contributors!

Thanks again for your generous support! We are now receiving 8057 USD/month (-2% from September) in recurring donations. This helps us cover the cost of our speedy CI and benchmarking servers, one of our latest Outreachy interns, and funding maintainer work that helps more people contribute to Servo, as well as feature development.

Sources indicate that servo is also on thanks.dev, and already 37 GitHub users (+0 from September) that depend on Servo are sponsoring us there. If you use Servo libraries like url, html5ever, selectors, or cssparser, signing up for thanks.dev could be a good way for you (or your employer) to give back to the community.

Recent findings suggest that we now have sponsorship tiers that allow you or your organisation to donate to the Servo project with public acknowlegement of your support. If you’re interested in this kind of sponsorship, please contact us at [email protected].

Use of donations is decided transparently via the Technical Steering Committee’s public funding request process, and active proposals are tracked in servo/project#187. For more details, head to our Sponsorship page.

Introducing @huggingface/kernels: 200+ WebGPU Kernels for Local AI

📅 01 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible.
  • Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.
  • It has been revealed that the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of our biggest goals on the WebAI team at Hugging Face is to make browser inference as fast and as user-friendly as possible. Getting there is a multi-layer effort: models need browser-friendly representations, runtimes need to build efficient execution looks, and the individual GPU operations at the bottom of the stack need to make the most of many different devices and browser implementations.

Today, we are releasing the first layer of that effort: @huggingface/kernels, a minimal library for loading and running optimized WebGPU kernels from the Hugging Face Hub, together with an initial collection of 207 kernels at huggingface.co/webgpu-kernels.

It has been revealed that the collection covers operations used across a wide variety of machine learning architectures and workloads. More importantly, each kernel is published as a complete, versioned package: its interface, shader templates, correctness cases, benchmark cases, and usage instructions all live together on the Hub.

Industry observers note that we are also launching Fleet, an in-browser GPU benchmarking and testing suite that runs and scores the kernels on your hardware. Beyond the results for your own machine, Fleet gives the community a way to contribute performance and correctness evidence from devices we could never cover in a conventional test lab. With your consent, every run adds private evidence that can help us find failures (incorrect results, pathologically slow cases, etc.), improve kernel variants, and make better optimization decisions across real-world hardware.

A model running in the browser eventually becomes a sequence of GPU operations: matrix multiplications, normalizations, convolutions, attention primitives, quantization operations, data-layout transformations, and many more. WebGPU makes these operations available across modern browsers through a portable API, while WGSL provides a common language for the shaders that execute them.

Portability, however, does not automatically mean performance. Two shaders can implement the same operation and produce the same output while behaving completely differently across different accelerators. Workgroup sizes, memory access patterns, vectorization, data types, and fusion strategies can all affect performance. The best choice can also change with the input shape, device, browser, and available WebGPU features.

It has been revealed that this is why kernels form a foundational layer of fast browser inference. Higher-level runtimes can only be as efficient as the operations they dispatch. By making those operations individually discoverable, testable, benchmarkable, and versioned, we can improve the foundation independently while keeping a stable contract for the layers above it.

Recent findings suggest that each kernel in the collection has its own repository and kernel card. The card documents the operation's semantics, inputs, outputs, attributes, supported data types, source files, and a ready-to-run @huggingface/kernels example.

It has been revealed that for example, ai.onnx.Add implements elementwise addition with multidirectional broadcasting. It is one of the simplest operations in a neural network, used everywhere from residual connections to adding a bias. Its card documents the two inputs, the broadcasted output shape, supported data types, and the variants available for different shapes and devices.

Behind the card, the repository contains the artifacts needed to understand and evaluate the implementation:.

This structure turns a shader into a reusable software artifact. The interface is inspectable without reading WGSL, correctness and performance cases travel with the implementation, and published versions can be loaded explicitly rather than depending on an unversioned file URL. Our kernels can also serve as reference implementations for developers building custom WebGPU kernels or integrating these operations into their own runtimes.

Running these kernels requires a browser with WebGPU support. WebGPU availability depends on the browser, operating system, GPU, and driver. You can check for it in JavaScript with "gpu" in navigator.

@huggingface/kernels provides the bridge between a kernel repository and your application. Call getKernel with a Hub repository ID and a contract version, then invoke the returned function with typed input data and tensor shapes. Here is a small bias-add example:.

The second input is broadcast across the first dimension, producing an output with shape [2, 3]. The loader derives that output shape and logical data type from the manifest contract and the inputs, then allocates c automatically.

Addition on six floats is deliberately the smallest possible demo. At this size, the GPU round trip costs far more than the math. The point is the call pattern: it stays exactly the same for the heavyweight operations where optimized kernels actually pay off, such as matrix multiplication (ai.onnx.MatMul). Only the repository ID and the inputs change.

According to recent reports, even this elementary operation illustrates why kernels need variants. Equal-shape addition can use a direct vectorized path, while broadcasted inputs need different indexing logic. The published Add kernel includes variants for equal shapes, vectorized broadcasting, scalar processing, and general broadcasting. The runtime can select an implementation that fits the current call and device without changing the application-facing API.

The version: 1 option selects version 1 of the published kernel contract. It is separate from an ONNX opset, an operator's since_version, or a model revision. Keeping those concepts separate lets applications depend on a stable JavaScript-facing contract while kernel implementations evolve behind it.

Recent findings suggest that so, how much of a difference do optimized kernels actually make? We put our collection head-to-head with ORT WebGPU on an Apple M4 GPU, using ONNX Runtime Web 1.30.0-dev.20260826-b1f76d586a. We started with 1,756 test cases across all 207 operations and kept the 809 cases where both sides produced matching outputs and reliable timings.

Across those comparisons, our kernels were 2.57x faster by geometric mean and 1.90x faster at the median, with 629 wins, 176 losses, and 4 ties. Here is a closer look at four familiar operations:.

Industry observers note that some individual wins were much bigger. A particularly difficult bilinear Einsum case (i,ij,j with size 4096) ran in 0.136 ms with our kernel versus 1,396 ms with ORT WebGPU: more than 10,000x faster. A row-wise CumSum over [256, 4096] was 301x faster, at 0.016 ms versus 4.784 ms. These are unusual cases rather than the speedups you should expect everywhere, but they show how much a specialized kernel can help when a general implementation hits a slow path.

We timed the work done on the GPU itself, leaving out setup such as loading kernels, creating sessions, uploading inputs, compiling shaders, and reading outputs back. Very short workloads are naturally harder to measure, and small cases can benefit from the GPU cache, so these numbers are best read as a useful comparison rather than a promise for every application.

Sources indicate that they are also results for individual operations, not complete models. Exact performance will change across GPUs and browsers, which is why Fleet is so important for building a broader picture.

We are also working with the ONNX Runtime team to upstream these improvements so they can benefit the broader ONNX Runtime Web ecosystem.

Sources indicate that webGPU performance varies across GPUs, browsers, and drivers, so results from one machine only tell part of the story. Fleet lets anyone run correctness and performance checks in the browser and see how the kernels behave on their hardware.

With consent, each run privately contributes evidence that helps us spot device-specific failures, compare variants, and improve selection rules. The goal is simple: use broad, real-world coverage to make the kernels faster and more reliable for everyone.

The initial 207 kernels are a starting point, not the end state. Publishing kernels independently on the Hub gives us a common place to inspect contracts, compare implementations, reproduce correctness checks, and improve performance without embedding every shader directly into every runtime.

The collection is also part of the Hub's broader kernel ecosystem: on the Kernels page, the WebGPU kernels sit alongside kernels for CUDA, ROCm, Metal, and other platforms, and can be filtered, sorted, and explored like any other artifact on the Hub.

The pieces reinforce one another:.

This is the low-level foundation for the next steps in our browser inference stack. We are excited to connect these kernels to higher-level model tooling, continue expanding operation coverage, and make fast local inference easier to use across the WebAI ecosystem.

Explore the WebGPU kernel collection, try @huggingface/kernels, and join the Fleet to contribute evidence from your device and help us make the kernels better for everyone.

The Fleet part may matter as much as the kernels. The 809 comparable cases on an M4 are useful, but browser, driver and device variance is where WebGPU tends to get painful. Will Fleet eventually expose per-device distributions, or is the strategy to use the runs only for aggregate selection rules?

In an automated build system, I could see per device kernels, made more interesting by fusion of ops.

In a recent development, the area that obviously needs more attention are the 947 tests that did not result in reliable output. This could be the test, it could be that the ORT WebGPU is wrong, or the newly introduced kernel is wrong, or the test harness had problems, hard to know from the outside. Perhaps the Fleet thing is meant to improve this.

Very excited to see such attention at making WebGPU first class in ML!

It has been revealed that @sroussey Agreed—the excluded 947 need a taxonomy before the 2.57× summary can travel. I'd want counts by operation and device for unsupported, ORT mismatch, fresh-kernel mismatch, and harness/timeout, with raw failing cases downloadable. Then Fleet can optimize only within a proven-correct compatibility envelope; fusion and per-device tuning become much safer.

Excellent! This will help our WebAI community continue developing highly optimized solutions. Many thanks @Xenova and @nico-martin for the great work you have been doing.

Government may apply TV license fee to streaming services to fund the BBC

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year.
  • A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.
  • The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its aims for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Controversial move could save the BBC by bringing in more than a billion in extra funding each year.

A study suggests extending the TV license to cover streaming services such as YouTube and Netflix could solve the BBC’s funding problems, netting it an extra £1.6 billion ($2 billion) per year by 2032.

The British government is due to publish a white paper by the end of this year outlining its aims for the BBC's license fee and Royal Charter, which expires at the end of 2027.

One of the options is to extend the license so that it is needed to access streaming platforms like Netflix, Disney+, or Amazon Prime Video.

This is unlikely to prove popular, but if the fee was held at the current level (£180, $236 per year) it would generate up to £1.6 billion extra a year for the corporation and would better reflect how audiences watch television, according to entertainment industry research biz Ampere Analysis.

It has been revealed that as any Brit knows, the BBC is funded primarily through the TV license, which is charged on a per household basis. A license is required to watch or record live TV on any broadcast channel, or access the BBC iPlayer for on-demand content. A license is not currently needed for on-demand streaming platforms.

In a recent development, the government is understood to believe the current license scheme is “outdated and no longer fit for purpose,” and is weighing several options to reform it. Scrapping it entirely looks unlikely for now: a committee found that other European countries that did so ended up with less stable funding for their public service broadcasters, and weaker independence from political interference.

It has been revealed that TV licensing is controversial, with some people resenting having to pay the BBC just for the right to watch television. In response, the government has tried to limit fee increases, and made the license free for some elderly people. Together, these moved have reduced the BBC's funding, leading to service cuts and further. dissatisfaction.

Responding to a report by the National Audit Office (NAO) that found the BBC will remain under financial pressure despite widespread cuts, the National Union of Journalists (NUJ) urged the government to secure the broadcaster's future in the next charter renewal.

"The BBC shouldn't be in this position. These cuts are the result of a decade of underfunding, with NAO identifying a 26 percent real-terms reduction in license fee income in the last nine years alone," remarked NUJ general secretary Laura Davison.

Sources indicate that many Brits no longer pay the license fee, preferring to watch only streamed content, or claiming that they do. Ampere states more than 90 percent of UK households watch live television, but only 84 percent of eligible households pay the fee, meaning a sizable number are freeloading. Extending the fee to cover on-demand and streaming services would close the loophole, it says.

Recent findings suggest that another option could see the license fee reduced to £150 ($196) in 2028, assuming perfect enforcement, analysts at Ampere say. They neglect to detail what this "perfect enforcement" mechanism consists of.

"Widening the remit of the license fee at current prices would significantly increase the BBC’s funding, strengthening its long-term financial position and ability to compete with local and global rivals," said Ampere Senior Analyst Sam Khoury.

Industry observers note that "Alternatively, in the context of ongoing cost of living pressures in the UK, the government could opt to reduce the price of the fee payable by the extended pool of consumers. Coupled with a reformed enforcement mechanism that effectively reduces evasion, this would still improve the BBC's financial outlook relative to the status quo.".

Earlier this year, the government revealed that it was planning for a switch-off of the broadcast digital terrestrial television (DTT) service in the future.

This is again because of the rapidly changing nature of the TV landscape, with viewers shifting to online streaming, creating a hybrid landscape between IPTV, traditional DTT, satellite broadcasting, and cable.

According to recent reports, current licenses for DTT services expire at the end of December, 2034, but the government may choose to extend them to 2044. ®.

AWS Weekly Roundup: Local Zone in Bogotá, 30-minute Lambda timeout, and more (November 24, 2026)

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1419 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does.
  • Two other threads ran through the week.
  • Recent findings suggest that headlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a newly introduced Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some limits shape architecture more than any feature does. AWS Lambda launched in 2014 with a 60-second timeout, moved to 5 minutes in 2015 and to 15 minutes in 2018, and then stayed there for eight years. Last week the limit doubled, and in the same week Lambda learned to run on GPUs and gave platform teams their own runtimes. That is a lot of Lambda for one week.

Two other threads ran through the week. A new AWS Local Zone in Bogotá brought AWS infrastructure closer to customers in Colombia. And AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS), Amazon Cognito, and Amazon CloudFront each shipped a piece of identity for agents: who an agent is when it shows up at your door, and how little it should be allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

Recent findings suggest that headlinesAWS Local Zone in Bogotá, Colombia – AWS opened a newly introduced Local Zone in Bogotá, so you can now run applications that need single-digit millisecond latency closer to users in Colombia. AWS Local Zones place compute, storage, and networking near large metropolitan areas with the same APIs and tools as a Region, for workloads like real-time gaming, live streaming, and financial transactions. The Bogotá Local Zone supports Amazon EC2 C7i, M7i, and R7i instances, Amazon EBS gp3, gp2, and io1 volumes with local snapshots, Amazon S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, AWS Direct Connect, and Application Load Balancer. To start, enable us-east-1-bog-1a in AWS Global View.

It has been revealed that AWS Lambda now supports a 30-minute timeout for on-demand Event Functions – You can now configure any Event Function with a timeout of up to 30 minutes (1,800 seconds), double the previous limit, for synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping invocations. On Lambda Managed Instances, synchronous invocations also go to 30 minutes, while asynchronous and event source mapping invocations keep the 90-minute timeout from September. Standard Lambda pricing applies, in all commercial Regions. Agentic requests that chain model and tool calls, media transcoding, and file conversion are the workloads AWS calls out. Before raising the value, read the considerations in the Compute blog post: a service that invokes your function synchronously applies its own timeout, client read and socket timeouts need to be longer, and a NAT gateway drops idle connections after 350 seconds, so long calls need keep-alives. For longer work, durable functions still run for up to a year, and now emit OpenTelemetry traces.

AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances – You can now run GPU-accelerated inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing as Lambda functions, packaged as OCI container images, with no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile. In the walkthrough, four concurrent requests shared one copy of the model on a single GPU and finished in about the same time as one. It’s optimized for inference with custom models, on G-series instances from G4dn to G6e. You pay the EC2 instance fee (Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply), a 9.75% management fee for GPU instances, and $0.20 per million requests.

Last week’s releases Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Amazon Polly now supports voice cloning – You can now create a custom voice in Amazon Polly from a few minutes of recordings of a consenting speaker, running on the Polly generative engine. It debuts in seven languages, including English, Spanish, and Portuguese, and each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. Polly doesn’t keep the recordings or train on them. Creating a voice is free, and you pay for the speech you synthesize. It’s a gated release, so request access through your account team. The ML blog post covers brand-voice use cases for contact centers, voice agents, and content.

According to recent reports, AWS Lambda now supports customer-managed runtimes – You can now manage a Lambda runtime as its own resource, separate from function deployment. Platform teams package approved SDKs, certificates, and security or monitoring agents as an OCI image in Amazon ECR, and functions pick up updates as Lambda recycles execution environments, with no per-function redeploys. Updates can be staged, with health metrics and rollback. There’s no additional charge, and the Compute blog walkthrough shows the platform-team workflow.

AWS STS announces GetScopedCredentials to scope down permissions at runtime – You can now take the temporary credentials a workload already holds and derive narrower ones, cutting permissions, session duration, or both. The result keeps the caller’s original identity, and permissions only ever narrow, so a sub-agent can never end up with more access than whoever created it. Access to the API is controlled with IAM policies, and every call lands in AWS CloudTrail. It’s available in all commercial Regions and beyond, including GovCloud (US) and China.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Cognito now supports dynamic client registration – You can now let MCP clients and AI agents register themselves at runtime (RFC 7591) instead of creating an app client in advance for each one. You choose between requiring an access token with a registration scope or opening registration to any client, and dynamically registered clients carry a client ID prefix so you can filter and manage them with the rest. It’s available on the Essentials and Plus looks, and client ID metadata documents arrived the same week.

Sources indicate that amazon CloudFront Functions now supports network calls – You can now call your own APIs from a function with cf.fetch() and act on the response, so authorization, personalization, or fraud checks that used to need Lambda@Edge or a trip to the origin can run at the edge. AWS’s own example: check an AI agent’s permissions and usage budget before the request reaches your API or MCP server. Network calls cost $0.10 per million on top of invocation charges and are included in the Pro flat-rate strategy and above. The Networking blog post also covers cf.beacon() for background analytics.

Sources indicate that amazon Aurora DSQL now supports multi-Region peering across continents – You can now build a multi-Region Amazon Aurora DSQL cluster with peers on different continents, such as US East (N. Virginia) and Europe (Ireland), and read and write to one strongly consistent database from both. It was a busy week for DSQL: PL/pgSQL functions and procedures arrived, and storage upgrades brought up to 50% higher write throughput at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Newly introduced with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

How the BMW Group governs hundreds of agents across thousands of developers – With more than 12,500 developers in R&D, BMW treats governance as deterministic code outside the agent’s reasoning loop, mostly in the CI/CD pipeline, so neither the agent nor its prompts can override it.

AI coding agents on Amazon EC2 Mac: How Cognition scales Devin for macOS – Cognition starts a fresh macOS VM for each Devin session in under a minute on Amazon EC2 Mac hosts across six Regions. The detail worth stealing: sessions are decoupled from hosts, and Cognition reports that about 90% release their VM when idle and resume from a snapshot in seconds.

How Klaviyo processes 3 billion daily events at scale with Amazon MSK Express – Timely reading for Black Friday week. Klaviyo moved from RabbitMQ to Amazon MSK Express brokers to absorb roughly 7 times normal event volume during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Running one set of processors across three priority topics, instead of separate infrastructure per level, cut costs by roughly 30%, according to the team.

AWS re:Invent – It’s next week: join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, or register for the free livestream to follow the keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.
